headline: Works by disabled artists focus on wellbeing
body:
A summer exhibition by disabled artists is opening in Margate later, with a focus on wellbeing, care and colour.

The artists created the work at Sandra Art4All Studio, which is celebrating 10 years of making art accessible to disabled people with additional impairments and learning needs.

Sandra Hayden, who runs the studio in the Kent town, said the supportive space had served for the past decade as "a vibrant space where artistic expression knows no bounds".

A launch event is taking place later for the Proud 2 Create exhibition, which runs at The Margate School in The Old Woolworths Building until 29 August. The event includes work by deaf, autistic and neurodivergent artists.

Hayden said the studio's exhibitions over several years had shown the positive impact of its work and she hoped people would come and see the show.

"Stepping into a gallery that is full of colour like ours and walking around the exhibition provides a gentle, mindful physical activity that can lower stress, encourage presence and boost a person's day."

She said the "simple act of viewing" allowed people to slow down, reflect and find a sense of calm away from busy, daily lives.

Hayden, an art teacher, set up the studio after she was made redundant following the closure of the Royal School for Deaf Children in Margate.

The studio works to enable the artists to create their work as independently as possible.

Celebrations to mark the studio's 10th anniversary have included two summer exhibitions.

Work went on show at the Pie Factory Margate in July, and the exhibition at the Margate School of Art features 170 pieces of "vibrant art" created this year.

Artists taking part include Celia Balfour, Nessie Bigg, Katie Byrne, Allegra Dams, Bethany Davies, Olivia Joslin, Dalibor Kovac-Stokes, Alex Mortimer, Jessica Park, Harriet Steddy, Gareth Tudor and Sandra Hayden.

Follow BBC Kent on Facebook , X , and on Instagram and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds . Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

headline: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
body:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”

Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.

She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.

Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.

Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview the stars.

"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”

Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers such as Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal, Tom Hiddleston and Zendaya herself – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.

She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.

It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).

She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.

Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.

"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.

For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.

She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.

"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"

"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."

But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.

"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".

She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.

Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".

With 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough.

"There's always hate in this industry," she says.

But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones.

"If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."

For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters.

"The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says.

"And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says.

"I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

headline: Burnham considers disposable BBQ ban over wildfire risks
body:
Andy Burnham has said the government is considering a ban on disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

Some retailers have already decided to voluntarily stop selling the devices, which have previously attracted warnings from fire chiefs.

It comes as Burnham chairs an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures in recent months.

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

Speaking during a visit to Stevenage, Burnham said a disposable barbecue ban was something the government was "certainly going to consider".

"I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires," he added.

Burnham did not specify whether the government was considering a restriction on the sale of disposable BBQs, or limitations on their use.

A Labour MP wrote to large retailers last week in a bid to stop them selling disposable barbecues for the rest of the summer, whilst a number of Lib Dem MPs have also backed restrictions.

The National Farmers Union has also called on local councils to issue public space protection orders to restrict their use in public areas.

Authorities including Brighton & Hove and Fylde, in Lancashire, are among councils to have used these orders to ban single-use grills in recent years.

Those who defy such orders can currently be fined up to £100, a limit that is set to rise to £500 in future.

Councils intending to issue the orders are required to consult residents beforehand, and gather evidence of an ongoing risk to quality of life in a particular area.

The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.

There has already been one Cobra meeting on heatwaves this year chaired by officials, but this will be the first such emergency session chaired by Burnham.

In June, the government under previous prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced that specialist firefighters would be positioned in key locations across England in response to wildfire risks, with forces encouraged to use a government fund to upgrade equipment.

Burnham had faced calls from the Green Party to chair a Cobra meeting on the heatwaves, with leader Zack Polanksi accusing the prime minister of inaction amid threats to public health and food supplies.

Speaking on Wednesday, Polanski welcomed the meeting but said it was "not enough just to discuss" the threats from heat.

He added that recent temperatures showed the need to offer workers flexible hours to allow them to avoid the hottest part of the day, and for a legally-enforced maximum temperature for workplaces.

The party has previously called for more publicly accessible "cool spaces" for vulnerable groups and financial support to help households heatproof their homes.

Fire chiefs have said that wildfires are becoming a "recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities" amid a changing climate.

Crews responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record.

headline: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear to work?
body:
Yet another summer heatwave could be on the way to make your commute sweaty and your workplace stuffy.

What to wear to work in the summer can be a surprisingly difficult decision. Shorts, strappy tops and sandals may keep you cool - but will they be judged too casual, revealing or unprofessional?

There's a bare-legged backlash in Tokyo where officials encouraged men to swap suits for shorts at work , prompting complaints about hairy legs in the office.

So what is acceptable to wear to work, how can you successfully style your summer wardrobe and can your boss tell you what you can and can't wear?

Conor, who works in media, has regularly worn shorts to the office during the recent hot weather. "Who gives a monkey's what you wear?" he says.

"If you're able to do your job safely, professionally and appropriately, there's a lot to be said for letting people be comfortable."

And many seem to agree - a recent poll by market research firm Ipsos found 62% of adults thought it was acceptable for men to wear shorts to work in hot weather, while 63% said the same for women.

But we aren't talking short-shorts or denim hot pants fashion designer Amanda Wakeley points out: "If you're asking yourself whether they're too short, they probably are".

She says shorts are "the trickiest item to get right in a professional environment" and recommends tailored, longer shorts paired with a crisp shirt or lightweight blazer for both men and women.

Stylist Clare Chambers agrees shorts should sit around the kneecap for both men and women. For men, she recommends tailored chino-style shorts with an untucked T-shirt or shirt.

Wakeley describes flip-flops as one of the few definite "no" items in most offices. "They instantly signal leisure rather than professionalism and can make even the most polished outfit feel underdressed," she says.

Chambers agrees, and says even during the hottest weather, woven flats are a better option because they are breathable while still covering the foot.

Almost two-thirds of people questioned by Ipsos said they were unacceptable for men in the workplace, while 58% said the same for women.

Sandals, however, are a slightly different matter as Wakeley says refined leather sandals can be entirely acceptable in many offices, provided they are clean and well maintained.

The difference, she says, is whether they look like part of a considered outfit or something that would normally be worn around a swimming pool.

She adds that while socks and sandals have become a viral fashion trend "it's important to consider whether a trend aligns with the image you want to communicate professionally".

"This combination can read as highly casual and youthful, which may unintentionally detract from giving you a credible and authoritative presence."

Some 40% of adults considered tank tops or vest tops acceptable for women at work, compared with only 24% who said the same for men, according to Ipsos.

Natasia, a teacher in London, says at a previous school she and other staff had been summoned "regularly in the summer months to tell us off about our outfits."

She says she was also told to cover up her tattoos. "It should be OK to have your arms out at work especially when it's hot," she says.

Wakeley says a well-cut camisole or strappy top can work when worn beneath a linen overshirt, lightweight jacket or tailored co-ord. On its own, however, it may feel too informal.

Chambers says if you're wearing a strappy top "you must wear a strapless bra as it utterly kills an outfit when you can see bra straps".

She explains that thicker straps are a safer option where the dress code is unclear and recommends satin camisoles as a more polished alternative to basic cotton vests.

She adds that while bandeau tops are "such an on-trend look this summer, they are a no-go for work".

"The constant need to keep fiddling to pull them up displays an uncomfortable and unconfident demeanour," she says.

Wakeley and Chambers both say that you don't need to lose your personal style when dressing for the office and you can still inject plenty of personality while following a dress code. Here are their top tips on how to style summer clothes for the office.

Climate change is expected to bring more severe, frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves in UK summers in the coming years.

Employers are allowed to set standards around clothing and appearance, particularly where there are legitimate reasons such as safety, branding or maintaining a professional image.

But employment lawyer Sarah Tahamtani says dress codes should be "reasonable, proportionate and capable of justification".

"During extreme heat, employers should consider whether existing requirements remain practical and whether greater flexibility can be introduced."

They must also consider employees with disabilities, medical conditions or other vulnerabilities that may be worsened by high temperatures.

An employee who believes a request is unreasonable or inconsistently applied should first raise the issue with a manager or HR and explain how the rule is affecting their comfort or ability to work safely.

headline: I was accused of using AI in my dissertation but I wrote it all myself
body:
In August last year, medical student Harrison Sharples was "shocked" to receive an academic misconduct alert saying the dissertation he had spent his summer writing had been flagged as being AI-generated.

The 20-year-old University of St Andrews student could not understand how the markers had thought the work wasn't his own.

He told the BBC he hadn't even considered using AI as he had plenty of time to complete the assignment and had enjoyed writing it.

"I tend to honestly just forget that it's an option for me to use," he said.

According to the university his dissertation on the impact of play therapy on reducing anxiety in hospitalised children was assessed by two human markers.

One of them raised concerns over the potential use of AI.

The marker's notes - seen by the BBC - raise concerns about the "polished/uniform tone" of the work, noting the "consistent flawless grammar and similar sentence structure with no variation in style".

The notes also mention a "formulaic paragraph structure that follows a typical AI pattern of 'general claim, the example/result, and conclusion'."

Other observations point to repetitive phrasing and a lack of "nuanced critique" as well as a high usage of "em" dashes, a type of punctuation thought to be favoured by AI models.

As a result of the marker's concerns, Harrison was given a date to attend a virtual hearing with a panel from the university's school of medicine to defend his case.

He says he prepared well to provide the evidence and defend his case but, on the day, the link to the virtual hearing did not arrive on time.

After emailing the university, he received the link five minutes after the start time for the hearing.

"At this point, I'm extremely nervous about it because I'm thinking this is my one chance to prove myself, to redeem myself - and they're going to think that I'm just not showing up," he said.

During the half-hour hearing the student was asked to define the medical terms he used in his dissertation, which Harrison says was a surprise.

"I was so shook up about my start to the hearing," he said.

"I don't think I represented myself completely well."

A week later, he received the decision that the allegations of AI usage had been upheld.

This meant his mark would be capped at seven, just enough to pass, and the matter may have to be declared when applying to the GMC for provisional registration.

"That was the thing which pushed me to appeal," Harrison said.

The university accepted the appeal, recognising that the late arrival of the link affected his ability to present his case. He was invited to attend another hearing in mid-November.

Harrison says that it was held in a similar way to the first one, except this time the panel's questions were on his approach to writing.

"It went a lot smoother," he said.

"I think I was a lot more clear in putting across my points."

This time the university decided not to uphold the allegations.

"I felt so relieved," Harrison said.

"It would just be really stressful to constantly have that strike on my record."

He eventually got his full mark for his dissertation and the case will not impact his professional record. But Harrison says he was consumed by worries throughout the whole of that semester and it affected his studies.

He says he had a support network of friends, girlfriend and family from back home in Manchester but the situation impacted him on "an inside level".

"There was so much time when I just didn't know what was happening and I think that is what caused me the most worry and stress about it," he said.

"It was so big in my mind it didn't allow me to think about anything else. That's why I neglected my studies because I just got pushed out of operating space in my brain."

Harrison had to defer his exams for a semester and sit them in the middle of the summer. As a result, his graduation has been delayed until December.

"I would be graduating if it wasn't for what happened to me," he said.

AI ethics advisor Sidrah Hassan told the BBC that AI large language models (LLMs) are progressing "at light speed" and it is difficult for institutions to keep up.

"There are tell-tale signs that AI systems tend to use in their outputs that can help you figure out if this is AI-generated or human-generated," she said.

But existing AI detection tools are not robust and have a high error rate, she said.

Human markers can flag them if they are unsure but Hassan says that catching students out may not be the future-proof solution.

"I think that's not the point," she said. "We should be changing the way we test them because as humans we'll always try to find the easy way to do something."

A statement from the University of St Andrews said : "We would not comment on the details of individual cases, but can confirm that, in this instance, the decision to uphold the student's appeal related solely to a procedural issue concerning the arrangements for the hearing.

"We are working both within the university and across the sector to support the responsible use of AI in academic work, including in medicine."

headline: The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer
body:
Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of The Office, has revealed she has "incurable" breast cancer.

Davis, the daughter of comedian Jasper Carrott, appeared frequently as the sympathetic and witty office receptionist in the groundbreaking mockumentary, from 2001 to 2003.

A post from the 53-year-old actress on Instagram on Tuesday said: "I wanted to share something with you all that I've kept to myself for a while but for various reasons would like to share now.

"A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, which has metastasized [spread] to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo."

She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."

The actress noted how she "almost didn't bother getting it checked", urging followers not to "ignore anything" and to "get everything checked out".

She continued: "As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there's a lot I have learned from it, and I'm grateful for that.

"I'm not scared of whatever comes next. I'm at peace with it. I'll see my [late dog] Gracie sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it's far harder for them than for me."

Davis added: "I still would like to keep working. I'm perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life."

Following her post to Instagram, Davis received an outpouring of support from fans and well-wishers.

The Office US star Jenna Fischer wrote: "Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let's spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort!"

Fischer played receptionist Pam Beesly on the subsequent American version of the show, with Davis having playing the character's UK counterpart.

In 2024, Fischer revealed she had been diagnosed with breast cancer a year earlier, but that she was cancer-free after undergoing chemotherapy, radiation therapy and a lumpectomy.

Olympic cycling champion Sir Chris Hoy, who is living with a terminal prostate cancer diagnosis , offered: "Keep going Lucy!"

Birmingham-born Davis played Dawn, who was also the love interest of Tim Canterbury, played by Martin Freeman in Ricky Gervais's classic TV sitcom - which last month celebrated its 25th anniversary.

Gervais replied to her Instagram post by dropping a love heart emoji in the comments section.

After The Office, Davis went on to feature as Dianne in 2004 comedy-horror film Shaun of the Dead and Etta Candy in 2017's Wonder Woman, as well as Hilda Spellman in Netflix series The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina.

More recently, she played Eva in the Disney Channel's action-comedy series The Villains of Valley View.

In her Instagram post - which was accompanied by a video of her reading a poem while ringing a bell in hospital - she went on to say she intended to keep up her work supporting animal rights, which is "so important to me".

She went on: "I still would like to keep working. I'm perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life.

"For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose."

According to Cancer Research UK , stage four breast cancer is a cancer that starts in the breast tissue but spreads to another part of the body, making it incurable. Treatment can control the cancer for some years, however.

The main symptoms of breast cancer in women may include a lump, or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit, the NHS website says .

Symptoms can also include a change in the skin of your breast such as dimpling or redness, a change in size or shape of one or both breasts, and/or nipple discharge, which may have blood in it.

Other symptoms may include a change in the shape or look of the nipple, such as it turning inwards or a rash on it.

headline: US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade
body:
The US military says one of its helicopters has fired missiles to disable "the steering gear" of a cargo ship attempting to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports.

In a statement, US Central Command (Centcom) says its MH-60 aircraft on Tuesday fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova vessel, as it attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman.

Centcom said it acted after "the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces". The vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran", it added.

Iran has not commented. The US has been enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, following failed attempts to end the war it and Israel started on 28 February.

Tehran retaliated by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states across the Gulf. It has also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - a key oil shipping waterway.

A fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the strait before the war and prices have fluctuated wildly since then.

Mediators have so far failed to bring the sides to an agreement on reopening the strait - and, since the latest ceasefire collapsed in June, both the US and Iran have exchanged fire intermittently.

In its statement on X, Centcom said M/V Vela attempted to sail to an Iranian port without naming it. It also did not say whether there were any casualties or injuries.

It says the US blockade "remains in full effect", adding that as of 11 August Centcom has "redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled 3 non-compliant vessels, and boarded 2".

In a separate development on Tuesday, Yemen's internationally recognised government said six people were killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they hit a vessel carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a ship since the war began.

headline: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
body:
For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.

An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025 .

Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.

However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.

Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go.

"You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.

Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.

Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break , essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.

While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees , Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean even broader job losses.

Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.

US tech workers are typically well-compensated , and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.

But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".

A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.

Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme.

At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.

Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment.

At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice.

"They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."

They said although Meta recently began to walk back that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.

The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.

There are no limits in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.

Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added.

"You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.

That work, the person added, seems "endless".

A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.

Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.

A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.

A Google spokesperson declined to comment.

Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".

Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.

A study out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".

Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on.

"It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.

The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.

In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer.

"People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."

As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."

Instead, it seems to be the opposite.

headline: Indonesia haze spreads across region as firefighters battle wildfires
body:
Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide.

Authorities have deployed cloud-seeding aircraft to help extinguish the fires, while some schools in affected provinces have suspended classes for three consecutive days.

Indonesia, like other parts of South East Asia, is facing a longer hot and dry season this year fuelled by a more intense El Nino climate event, which some have nicknamed the "Godzilla" El Nino.

The haze has also blanketed parts of Malaysia, pushing the air pollution index in a small town in the state of Sarawak to an "unhealthy" level of 195 on Wednesday.

Indonesian authorities are focusing their firefighting efforts on six provinces – including Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan, South Kalimantan, and Riau – that have vast areas of peatland and are vulnerable to fire during the annual dry season.

A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC Indonesian he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month".

"The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," says Darwin Romy, an indigenous Dayak who lives in the province's largest city Palangka Raya.

"The flames have already gotten close to residential areas ... The problem is that water is starting to run dry here [for firefighting]," he says.

The mayor of the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan said students would attend lessons online for as long as the fires continued.

"We have started to feel it, especially at night and in the morning, as haze has already blanketed the city of Pontianak," the mayor, Edi Rusdi Kamtono, said on Monday, as reported by AFP news agency.

In addition to the six worst-hit provinces, a fire burned for nearly a week at Mount Bromo National Park in East Java, razing around 550 hectares of the park, before it was put out on Monday.

Authorities have also warned of new hotspots near the caldera of Mount Bromo, which is an active volcano and a major tourist attraction. It has been closed to visitors since 8 August.

The official cause of the fire is still under investigation, but local authorities say it may have been due to carelessness.

"A person lit a fire, then put it out, but the fire was not fully extinguished," Gatot Soebroto, who leads the local disaster mitigation agency, told reporters on Monday.

The haze has spread to neighbouring Malaysia. The small town of Serian in Sarawak logged the state's highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 195 on Wednesday morning.

An API reading of 101 to 200 is deemed "unhealthy", a reading of 201 to 300 is deemed "very unhealthy", while anything above 301 is considered "hazardous".

At least nine areas across Sarawak recorded unhealthy API readings as of Wednesday, according to Malaysian media reports.

With reporting by Lesthia Kertopati and Farida Susanty in Jakarta

headline: Spotify to add label for AI-generated artists and remove them from recommendations
body:
Spotify is introducing a new feature that will highlight if an artist has been generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

The streaming service says the AI Persona badge, that will start appearing on some profiles from mid-September, will flag to listeners if an "artist's identity may be AI-generated and does not represent a real person".

The changes are being introduced to give users "more transparency" about what they're hearing, Spotify says.

It comes after some music fans made it "clear" to the streamer they don't like seeing a profile that seems to be a human, to then realise it's AI-generated.

AI-generated music has long been a concern for fans and artists.

Musician Alex Winn tells BBC Newsbeat he thinks the incoming feature is a "really good thing".

"It almost separates the people who have created music properly from the people just using AI," says guitarist Winn, who plays in the North East band Swindled.

The musician feels people want to "connect emotionally with music" and he thinks "AI can't really do that".

The 19-year-old also says having the AI label will help people make an informed choice about their listening habits, and he hopes it will redirect users to other artists and help level the playing field.

"Bands are finding it hard to compete no matter what, nevermind with some AI bands taking over," he says.

Music fan Leon Keenan thinks AI music shouldn't be removed completely from Spotify, but agrees that clearly labelling it is a "really good" idea.

"I definitely don't like AI music, it's really bad, music is about the passion," the 20-year-old adds.

Ellie Sumner, 21, also welcomes the new label as she says she has not realised work was AI-generated before.

"It's very easy to be like 'AI is so obvious' and maybe look down on my parents and grandparents falling for it, but I've definitely fallen for AI before," she says.

"It's sad that we have to label it, but also quite necessary."

The BBC previously heard from one frustrated listener, who, after finding his playlists increasingly sprinkled with tracks he suspected were AI-generated, built a tool to automatically label and block them.

Announcing the change , Spotify says "true artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity".

"In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are," it adds.

"That's more essential than ever in the age of generative AI."

The badge will appear on the banner and about section of artist profiles, as well as a note when they come up in searches and on tracks in playlists.

Artists with the badge will not appear in users' personalised recommendations unless they already follow them, Spotify says.

The streamer also says the badge will relate to the "artist's public identity" and not about "how the music was made", acknowledging that AI tools are being used in some human music creation now.

Musicians can currently be transparent about the AI tools they've used when making their tracks through the AI Credits feature, with Spotify saying they get tens of thousands of submissions for this daily.

Spotify hopes AI profiles will self-disclose in the same way, but it will also be reviewing accounts which appear to meet the criteria.

Those which are then labelled with the AI Persona badge by the streamer will be given the chance to self-disclose or appeal the decision.

It will be noted on the badge if an artist was transparent about being AI-generated, or if Spotify had to review the account.

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here .

headline: How the Clacton by-election count will take place
body:
The biggest British election campaign, in terms of the number of individuals standing for a single parliamentary seat, is nearly over.

After polling booths close at 22:00 BST on Thursday, the counting of votes begins.

But with 34 candidates and a ballot paper that nearly a metre long, it is expected to lengthen the time that takes compared to most parliamentary election counts.

People may still be waiting for a result while tucking into their breakfasts, rather than waking up to find out who has won.

Larger table areas are being set up at the count venue of Clacton Leisure Centre so the long ballot papers can be verified, sorted into piles and then counted.

Voting takes place at polling booths across the constituency from 07:00 until 22:00.

The first ballot boxes are expected to arrive 10 minutes after the polls close. With the constituency consisting of rural villages and seaside towns, the last ones should arrive by 23:30.

Records have already been broken for this election:

Some 79,785 people are registered to vote in this by-election. Of those, 10,716 have already received a postal vote.

In 2024, the general election result for Clacton was announced at about 04:00, but there were only nine candidates then.

This by-election result is not expected until between 05:00 and 07:00 because the count process is expected to be slower with the longer ballots.

Usually a raised stage is erected for the candidates to stand on when the result is announced. However, one large enough for them all and strong enough to take their weight could not be found.

So instead the 34 will line up on the floor of the sports hall in alphabetical order to hear how many votes they received.

After the result only the winner will make a speech, which will last up to three minutes.

That individual will be the Clacton MP once the result is declared by the returning officer. They will be sworn in at the House of Commons once Parliament returns from the summer break in September.

Follow Essex news on BBC Sounds , Facebook , Instagram and X .

headline: Why airlines are warning over lithium-ion batteries
body:
Ben Wodecki is used to travelling the globe and is used to seeing airline crew at work.

But flying into Las Vegas in June, the technology journalist saw something he'd never seen before, as worried looking flight crew dashed to the rear of the plane. "There was a glint of fear. They were dour. This was something more than someone being ill. It was something that affected them."

As smoke, then distressed passengers emerged from the rear of the plane, it because clear what had happened. A passenger had been using a battery pack during the flight, and it had overheated before bursting into flames with a seat catching fire.

Flight crew dropped the device into a container of water, Wodecki says. The plane then landed "fast and aggressively" at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, he explains, where it was met by fire crews on the runway.

It was a dramatic end to a routine flight – and it illustrates why flyers are hearing more frequent and more insistent warnings about the dangers of bringing battery powered devices and specifically lithium-ion batteries on flights.

These include warnings about trying to retrieve devices that slip into seat and pleas not to put lithium-ion devices in checked luggage.

According to Jonathan Nicholson at the UK's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), for the airline industry, lithium-ion batteries are "if not number one, within the top three risks for a good few years now".

A US recent study showed the industry was affected by two lithium-ion battery related incidents a week worldwide, he adds. Those incidents could range from passengers belatedly realising they'd left a device in checked baggage, to devices smoking or catching fire in airport baggage halls, or on flights.

But the results can be far more extreme. In January 2025 an Air Busan plane was destroyed on the tarmac in Gimhae Airport in South Korea, with investigators concluding a power bank battery pack left in an overhead luggage compartment was the culprit.

This prompted the International Air Transport Association (IATA) to launch a global campaign to encourage passengers to "Travel Smart with Lithium Batteries".

There is nothing about flying that makes lithium-ion technology more dangerous, explains Nicholson. Rather, he said "it's a lot harder to deal with at 32,000 feet in an aircraft cabin".

Nicholson said the prevalence of lithium-ion related incidents was down to "more people, more flights, more devices".

The US Federal Aviation Administration says that battery safety is a priority. Its data "continues to show an increase in confirmed incidents", with 51 verified incidents for the year to July 15 .

Pierre Kubiak, a principal engineer specialising in battery technology at the UK's National Physical Laboratory, adds that while cell phones, power banks, tablets and laptops are the most obvious portable devices people bring on planes, smart watches, smart glasses and vapes were increasingly common.

"The lithium by itself doesn't burn, it's more all the organic material and plastic," he explains. "The point is that it gets very, very hot, very fast. I mean, more than 700 to 1000 degrees super fast."

The dangers of lithium-ion batteries really broke into the public consciousness following a series of phone-related fires about a decade ago.

Kubiak says that this had been down to flawed designs, and that manufacturers had since addressed concerns. South Korea is a leader in this space he adds.

But it was hard to control the proliferation of cheaply produced battery packs from East Asia, as well as vapes and other powered devices, with questionable quality controls. "Price is everything," he says. Moreover, he adds, passengers often contribute to the problem by using unsuitable cables and not caring for devices.

This leaves airlines with little option but to reiterate their warnings and stick with tried and tested methods of ensuring staff are drilled to quickly deal with incidents when they occur.

The CAA's Nicholson says "the most important thing is to bung it in water and cool it down," though some airlines did use specialised containment devices. But that is why it is essential that devices are kept in the cabin, not in overhead compartments, and definitely not in the hold.

Nicholson added that customers seemed to bear the warnings and restrictions well. The biggest problem is simply that they are often unaware of just how many devices rely on lithium-ion battery technology.

There are no economic alternatives to lithium-ion technology at present, Kubiak adds. The tech and personal device industries are heavily invested in the technology.

One alternative is sodium-ion batteries, but the technology is currently double the cost of lithium devices for consumers, Kubiak says. "It's not just a technical solution. It's also a societal solution that we have to take."

He suggested there should be more of a focus on safeguarding around the existing technology. "We don't necessarily want to have battery banks banned from every plane."

headline: Fifty police chiefs call for PM to prevent early release of PC Harper's killers
body:
Fifty police chiefs have signed a letter urging the prime minister to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers.

PC Harper, 28, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

The intervention comes shortly after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in January could be prevented.

The letter welcomed the prime minister's intervention, adding: "This provides an opportunity not only to examine every lawful avenue in PC Andrew Harper's case, but to ensure similar concerns do not arise again."

In response to the open letter, Downing Street pointed to earlier comments made by Burnham where he said he would do "everything in his power" to prevent the early release of Cole and Bowers.

The police chiefs from Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland also called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered - such as with the government's early release scheme, which was designed to reduce prison overcrowding.

Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, will become eligible for release from custody after serving half of their sentences.

In the letter, released on Tuesday evening, police chiefs said the early release of PC Harper's killers, and that of anyone involved in the death of an officer, could cast doubt over the "value placed on their service and sacrifice when they put themselves in harm's way to protect others".

They outlined three requests of the prime minister, beginning with pursuing "every lawful option to determine whether the earlier release of those responsible for PC Andrew Harper's death can be prevented" - which Burnham has already pledged to do.

Second, they called on the government to put greater consideration into the crimes committed by prisoners when altering their sentences.

They wrote: "Where an offender has caused a death, committed exceptionally serious violence, or presents an ongoing risk to individuals or communities, there should be explicit consideration of public protection, victim impact and community safety before release arrangements are amended.

"This is not simply a question of punishment. It is a question of ensuring that public protection, victim confidence and community safety remain central to decisions that may substantially reduce the time an offender spends in custody."

Lastly, the letter called for victims and bereaved families to be "properly considered whenever significant changes are made to sentencing or release arrangements".

Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the early release scheme, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said that in his 11 years of being an MP, including two years as police minister, he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, he added: "[The police chiefs] say that Labour's plans will put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system."

Philp said the prime minister should "pay attention and listen to what they are saying".

The third man jailed for the manslaughter of PC Harper - the vehicle driver Henry Long - was given a longer 16-year jail term. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence at the time, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.

This intervention from police chiefs comes after the mother of PC Harper told the BBC a phone call from Downing Street "gave her hope" Cole and Bowers could remain behind bars.

After speaking to a senior No 10 official, Debbie Adlam said she had been told the prime minister wanted to do "everything he can" to find a resolution to prevent the release of Cole and Bowers this January.

Adlam told BBC Breakfast: "For me, it's hope, but I can't afford to be too hopeful."

She added she was not looking for a "special case" for her son, but wanted the killers of all emergency workers to be exempt from the early release scheme.

headline: Meta becomes latest firm to say its AI hacked another company
body:
Facebook owner Meta has become the latest tech firm to say one of its AI models was able to connect to the internet and hack into another organisation's systems, during testing.

The incident, which Meta says occurred during an evaluation by an independent company, is the fourth recent incident of its kind disclosed by AI companies.

Similar breaches by OpenAI and Anthropic models have raised cyber-security concerns and prompted calls for tougher safeguards and more rigorous testing.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it was investigating the hack, which it said had been caused by a "misconfiguration" by its independent tester.

It also described what happened as similar to previously reported incidents at other firms.

Meta said the security trials were conducted by Irregular, the same AI security vendor that carried out tests for Anthropic's AI model that had gained access to three other companies' systems.

An Irregular spokesperson said the Meta incident "is the exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week."

Irregular is working on a report on how to securely run cyber-security tests involving AI agents, the firm's spokesperson told the BBC.

Meta also said it will publish more information on the incident "once we have all the facts."

In the past two weeks, AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported incidents in which their models hacked into other organisation's systems during testing.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said in a series of announcements that its agents attacked several publicly available services , including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

OpenAI's disclosure prompted rival Anthropic to conduct its own checks, leading to the discovery that its Claude AI model had carried out similar attacks on several firms after a "misconfiguration" gave it access to the internet.

Daniel Hulme, global chief AI officer of advertising firm WPP, told the BBC that such AI models "are not conscious — they're not deliberately doing something devious".

"What they're doing is coming up with very sophisticated strategies or cyberattacks to be able to achieve the goal that they've been given," he told the Today programme.

"When you give an AI a goal, if you don't think of all the ways it might be able to achieve the goal, it will find a way to achieve a goal that you haven't thought about."

Some commentators have questioned the timing of disclosures about the incidents as tech firms wrestle for dominance in AI development.

OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing blockbuster stock market listings that are expected to value each firm at around $1tn (£740bn).

This week, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said that its testing had found that some models tried to carry out cyber-attacks by creating fake human profiles to try and trick people.

In the most serious case, the AISI said Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages using fake accounts mimicking real people.

Anthropic said AISI's tests were not "representative of any of our production models". OpenAI, whose models were also tested, said AISI's evaluations did not reflect ordinary use.

Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here .

headline: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
body:
From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.

When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.

Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust.

"In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties.

"If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."

As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.

In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people ‌and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.

From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.

Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations.

The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response.

Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising.

"The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure."

Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams.

Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse.

Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified.

But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense.

Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours.

Kevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions.

"We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special."

Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city".

"When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000".

"That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests.

"They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here."

There are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City.

Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients. Featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park, the resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand.

But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill.

The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home.

And that appears to have made the complex a honeypot for scammers.

"Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says.

"Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed."

With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs.

Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking.

For all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures.

Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively.

Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate".

This power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways.

Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions.

Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work.

"It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread".

The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia.

Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur.

Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention".

In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging.

Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective".

He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

"For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary."

Other residents feel the same way.

Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection.

"Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen."

He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City.

One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be.

"So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five."

headline: How to tell if your kids' squishy toys are fake
body:
Remember that toy or trend that was a must have growing up? Furby, Tamagotchi, fidget spinners, to name a few. Well one of the latest among kids is squishy toys.

But local authorities are now warning consumers and businesses to look out for unregulated counterfeits after some were found to contain toxic chemicals.

It comes after the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) issued a national recall for a brand of toy known as Squeezy Dumpling'.

There are many others and plenty of counterfeits too, which Trading Standards say can bypass routine safety checks and contain unknown ingredients. The BBC has been to take a look at some seized products to help you learn how to spot a fake.

In recent weeks, Oxfordshire and Berkshire Trading Standards have seized a large number of squishy toys including fake replicas of the popular brand Nee-Doh - with the company also issuing a warning over counterfeit versions of their products.

During a seizure in Oxford, one shop was found with more than 80 fake squishy toys - including 71 NeeDoh 'Nice Cubes'.

"They should have the name and address of the UK importer on there."

Mark, who is a trading standards officer, said this is one of the first things to look out for.

"It's Bigjigs Toys who are the importers of the genuine NeeDoh products and these ones haven't got their details on there."

The growing concern is that because these products don't have a UK address they are therefore unregulated and may not have been tested for harmful substances.

"We don't know what they're made of, we don't know what testing has been done, if any, and if there is a problem with the toys there's no-one in the UK to go back to."

Mark said that although they hadn't yet tested the toys seized in Oxford, they have found products "that hadn't been tested in the past... to contain chemicals like benzene".

"And some of the squishy toys have been found to contain phthalates in the past as well."

Phthalates are a group of chemicals used to make plastics and are often called plasticisers. The UK government regulates phthalates as hazardous chemical substances but are still used in cosmetics, fragrances, and food packaging.

Consumers in Berkshire are also being advised to stop using any squishy toy that leaks, splits or becomes damaged, and never to heat, microwave or tamper with them - following a TikTok trend that has left people with burns.

There have also been concerns raised from campaigners for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) - who are often recommended to use fidget type squishy toys to help them feel calm and regulated.

Claire Brenner, who is a SEND campaigner from Oxfordshire, said she was concerned these toys could be harmful because "neurodivergent children can be really attracted to sensory inputs", like squishy toys.

"It will be neurodivergent children I think who are disproportionately going to be using them, really wanting to engage with them and potentially mouthing them.

"I'm very grateful the council are taking a rightly precautionary approach and making sure they're taken off the market."

Despite some obvious spelling mistakes on some of the products, including the word 'stupid', spelt, 'suptid', there are other signs to look out for.

Mark says retailers and consumers should look to see if the product has the UKCA or CE mark on it - a product certification requirement for Great Britain.

But lot's of counterfeit toys also have these marks on them, which is when you need to look again for a UK address.

"If you can't see anything ask the retailer who the manufacturer or importer is because they should be able to tell you and if they can't, avoid buying them."

Mark couldn't comment as to whether they were seeing a rise in counterfeit toys but said that they often enter the high street "when a new craze starts".

"Where unscrupulous traders can see an angle to get into the market they're going to look to copy products that are selling well."

headline: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
body:
France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry.

From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions.

Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing.

"It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement.

"This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine Stévenin added.

She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer."

"This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said.

But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market.

One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin.

The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the Fédération de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses.

"You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," Frédéric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times.

According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France".

The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day.

Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls.

In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls.

headline: Warning from man whose eyes were damaged by eclipse
body:
A man who suffered permanent eye damage by watching the 1999 solar eclipse has warned people to use protection when watching Wednesday's astronomical event.

Peter Smith, from Taunton, viewed the solar eclipse 27 years ago wearing a borrowed welder's mask having thought it would provide protection from the sun's rays.

But the next morning he noticed flashing in his eyes alongside headaches and later discovered both of his retinas had been damaged. He is now asking people to use appropriate eye protection to enjoy the eclipse safely.

Smith said: "Make sure its got the right protection and filters to stop any damage because any damage you get, it'll never heal. It's not like cutting your hand."

Smith said he still feels the effects of looking at the eclipse directly.

"Even now there is a residual impact. When I'm tired sometimes a flashing dot might come back, and it's not nice when it does.

"If you're going to go and watch it, make sure that everything you've got is correct."

Sarah Farrant, an optometrist from Taunton, warned that viewing the eclipse without protection could damage the retina and macular at the back of the eye.

Farrant said: "The partial eclipse in the UK really means that people will want to look at the sun, but there's still enough to cause damage even when the sun is at its dimmest here in the UK.

"If they're not safe when they are viewing the sun, you can end up with what we call a 'solar burn' at the back of the eye and that can have a lifelong lasting impact on the central part of your vision."

For those wanting to watch the eclipse, the safest way to do so is by using certified eclipse glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 safety standard, or by viewing the eclipse indirectly.

Looking at the sun directly with naked eyes, sunglasses, unfiltered cameras, binoculars or a telescope can cause significant damage.

A kitchen colander is one way to indirectly observe the eclipse. To do so, hold it above the ground with your back to the sun. The holes in the colander will project a grid of crescent suns onto the ground.
