headline: Nicholas Hoult joins Harry Potter TV show - see the cast so far
body:
Nicholas Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, has been cast in the hotly anticipated Harry Potter TV series.

The English actor, 36, will play Hogwarts professor Gilderoy Lockhart - who was portrayed by Sir Kenneth Branagh in the films.

The TV adaptation of JK Rowling's best-selling books will reach screens this Christmas, although Hoult will not be seen until season two.

In the stories, Lockhart was a celebrity author of books such as Magical Me before joining Hogwarts as a Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher in Harry's second year.

HBO announced the casting by quoting the title of Lockhart's autobiography and one of his famous lines: "Magical me indeed. Now, how many autographs would you like? Nicholas Hoult has been cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two of the new HBO original Harry Potter series."

Hoult found fame alongside Hugh Grant in the big-screen adaptation of Nick Hornby's novel About A Boy in 2002, before going on to star in teen drama Skins.

He played Hank McCoy, also known as Beast, in four X-Men movies, was Lex Luthor in the recent Superman film, was nominated for an Emmy for The Great, starred in Oscar-nominated film Nosferatu, and played the lead role in a biopic of author JRR Tolkien.

He is the latest name to join the cast for the TV version of Harry Potter, which is expected to last for a decade.

The show's first season - named Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone after the UK title of Rowling's first book - will be launched on HBO Max on 25 December.

The author's seven books were published between 1997 and 2007, and were turned into eight films from 2001 to 2011.

Rowling has since also become known for her outspoken views on the issue of gender identity. She says she is defending women's rights and has denied accusations of transphobia.

Many of the TV show's adult cast members have fielded questions in recent years about whether they support her stance, and taken varying positions.

The subject was in the headlines again this week when Bel Powley, who plays Petunia Dursley, told the Telegraph she "strongly disagrees" with the author.

headline: Swinney calls for Burnham rethink on Chinese factory in Highlands
body:
First Minister John Swinney has dismissed any suggestion he is prioritising political point scoring over national security after calling for Labour ministers to reconsider a Chinese firm's plan to build a wind turbine factory in the Highlands.

Ming Yang's proposed £1.5bn plant at Ardersier, near Nairn, was blocked by the UK government , citing unspecified national security concerns.

Swinney said he wanted Prime Minister Andy Burnham to re-examine the scheme to see if the concerns could be overcome.

It came after UK Energy Security Minister Michael Shanks accused the first minister of making a "political intervention against the country's national security".

He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast it was "surprising" that Swinney was calling for the Ming Yang plan to be reconsidered since he had received a national security briefing about the plan.

Ming Yang has described the UK government's decision - on what would have been the UK's largest wind turbine factory - as a "significant missed opportunity", saying it could have supported up to 1,500 jobs.

Aman Wang, the company's UK chief executive, said: "We fully respect the government's duty to protect national security, and have always been clear that we will meet the requirements the UK sets."

Responding to criticism from Shanks, Swinney acknowledged there were national security concerns.

However, he insisted he was taking an "intensely responsible approach by asking for a further examination of whether there are opportunities to take forward that development".

The first minister told the BBC that the factory would benefit everyone in Scotland and support the government's net-zero energy goals.

Asked if he was putting political point scoring ahead of national security, Swinney said he wanted the new prime minister to re-examine the proposals to ensure there was "no stone left unturned" to see if it could go ahead.

Ming Yang's plan was rejected by the UK government in March after ministers said they had to ensure it was "safe and secure".

The government also said the turbines from the factory would not be suitable for UK offshore wind projects and it could not support their use.

At the time, then Deputy First Minister Kate Forbes criticised "dithering" on the decision but said national security was important and must be respected.

She added that it was "regrettable" the UK government had not explained its decision to Ming Yang.

In April, Swinney accused the UK government of "an anti-Scottish move", adding that Labour ministers were "welcoming Chinese investment into Hinkley power station south of the border".

He has since written to Burnham, urging him to reconsider the proposal.

Shanks, speaking to BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast , said he had arranged for Swinney to have a security briefing following his comments in April.

He said it was therefore "surprising" that "having had that security briefing" the first minister was continuing to pursue the matter.

The Scottish Labour MP told the programme: "I think it is for him [Swinney] to answer why he is balancing what seems to be a political intervention against the country's national security.

"I think it is irresponsible for the first minister to do that."

He added: "There is no inherent reason why the UK government would not want to see jobs created in the north of Scotland either, so I hope people would take it on face value when I say there are national security implications.

"That is a legitimate reason for us to say no to a particular investment."

Ardersier is a former oil and gas fabrication yard which at its peak employed about 4,500 people, before closing in 2001 as demand dropped.

The 450-acre (182ha) site is currently being redeveloped and forms part of the Inverness and Cromarty Firth Green Freeport.

Prof Steve Tsang, director of the Soas China Institute at the University of London, said all Chinese companies are ultimately "answerable to the Communist Party of China", adding: "And that's where the security risk is."

He told BBC Scotland News that Chinese firms operating in other countries could be asked to help survey or disrupt infrastructure.

Prof Tsang said that while checks and regulations could be enforced on imported wind turbines from China, the same stringent checks could not be imposed on products made in the UK.

Why did the UK government not want the project at Ardersier to go ahead? Well, that's classified.

We know it had something to do with security concerns, but beyond that broad explanation it's difficult to know what the specific red flags were.

Michael Shanks seemed to suggest that John Swinney knows fine well why this project can't proceed.

But my understanding is that while the Scottish government doesn't dispute that the first minister got a security briefing, they feel this was more about general concerns around China, not the particulars around Ardersier.

Their view is that they haven't been shown a smoking gun, and therefore they want Andy Burnham to see if it's possible to overcome any security concerns he has.

Comparisons have been made with the Chinese super embassy in London, where the UK government said risks could be managed.

It seems to be the position of UK ministers that mitigation isn't possible in this scenario. And they seem to be insisting that John Swinney has all the information he needs to appreciate this.

headline: Jasper Carrott says family is 'so proud' of Lucy Davis after cancer diagnosis
body:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, who was one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

In a statement on Instagram on Tuesday, Davis explained: "A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer, which has metastasised to my bones.

"Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn't bother getting it checked. So I guess I'm saying don't ignore anything - get everything checked out."

She added: "As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can... I'm not scared of whatever comes next. I'm at peace with it."

As well as The Office, Davis has appeared in Shaun of the Dead, Wonder Woman, The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip and BBC Radio 4's The Archers.

After posting her statement, Davis received support from her Office co-stars including creator Ricky Gervais.

Actress Jenna Fischer, who played the same role as Davis in the US version of the sitcom, wrote: "Beautiful post. Love you lots."

US actress Sarah Paulson, who appeared opposite Davis in Studio 60, said: "Sending you love love love, you are and always have been full of magic."

Other stars sending support included Ulrika Jonsson, Amanda Abbington, Edgar Wright, Piers Morgan and Sir Chris Hoy, the Olympic cycling champion who was diagnosed with stage four prostate cancer, who wrote: "Keep going Lucy."

According to Cancer Research UK, stage four breast cancer is a cancer that starts in the breast tissue but spreads to another part of the body, making it incurable. Treatment can control the cancer for some years, however.

The main symptoms of breast cancer in women may include a lump, or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit, the NHS website says.

Symptoms can also include a change in the skin of your breast such as dimpling or redness, a change in size or shape of one or both breasts, and/or nipple discharge (if you are not pregnant or breastfeeding), which may have blood in it.

Other symptoms may include a change in the shape or look of the nipple, such as it turning inwards or a rash on it.

headline: 'I've had to Botox my CV': Are AI recruitment tools affecting women's careers?
body:
The fear of becoming surplus to requirements because of advancements in AI is one shared by millions of workers, but are AI recruitment tools posing a specific threat to women trying to return to employment?

After a career spanning decades, with senior corporate roles in fashion, and a period of freelancing, 52-year-old Stacey Duguid decided to find "one last job".

What followed was 16 months of sending "gazillions" of CVs, with little more than a handful of automated replies, despite never previously struggling to find work.

Feeling "lonely and shameful" and wondering if it was a "me problem", she posted on social media asking whether other women her age were having the same experience.

The response was overwhelming, with thousands of women saying they were facing similar struggles.

Stacey, who lives in north London, believes AI-powered recruitment tools could be contributing to the problem and has "Botoxed" her CV by removing references to her age and experience.

"AI holds a mirror up to society. It's a reflection of our bias," she said.

"I'm not saying this is just a women's issue; I've had messages from men too. My point is about gendered ageism."

The BBC has since spoken to more than 60 women aged 40 to 65 across a range of industries who have been struggling to find work.

Most have decades of experience in senior roles and say they've submitted countless CVs, only to receive automated rejections or no response at all.

Like Stacey, many believe AI recruitment tools are playing a role.

Koeyli Jaluka, 49, has held senior roles across manufacturing, corporate and healthcare.

"I've never been in this position before. For the last 10–12 years I've been headhunted. Now I'm hunting for jobs and being relentlessly rejected."

Made redundant nine months ago, she's applied for 442 jobs and has heard back in only a few cases. She's occasionally been told she's "too senior" – which she believes is "code for old". Despite two decades of experience and two degrees, she says her confidence has "taken a hit".

She believes tighter budgets, AI screening and increasingly narrow hiring criteria are all contributing.

"A lot of us have been told by career coaches to shave off the first 10 years of work on our CVs just to ensure we don't come across as having worked for too long."

Anna Cowie, 52, had a 30-year career in advertising but has been unemployed for almost four years.

She's lost count of the number of CVs she's sent, despite having never previously been without a job.

After decades of working for big brands, most recently helping to launch the new Battersea Power Station, she's now on jobseeker's allowance.

Anna has turned to volunteering for community festivals, and has found networking with real people a much more promising approach.

"You're seen as a human and not just lines on paper."

While it is impossible to know in many cases whether AI tools played a role in a screening or a rejection because employers rarely disclose details of their recruitment processes, there are widespread fears that AI recruitment tools are disadvantaging mid-life women .

The City of London Women Pivoting to Digital Taskforce, which focuses on women in the financial and professional services sector, has raised concerns about the growing use of AI in recruitment and its impact on women.

Chair Caroline Haines said the taskforce's research found significant concern that AI used to screen job applications and CVs does not recognise the skills many experienced women can bring.

"There is a high level of concern that AI at initial recruitment level... doesn't account for the skills of a vast body of women that could be very effective and therefore promote economic growth," she said.

For example, women who have taken time out of work for childcare may have gaps in their CVs that some AI screening systems could interpret negatively.

In terms of the bigger picture, the taskforce estimates AI and automation could displace hundreds of thousands of women's jobs by 2035.

Using data from Market and skills projections: 2020 to 2035, Department for Education , the taskforce estimates that without significant investment in retraining, firms could face more than £750m in severance costs.

In the digital taskforce's recent survey of over 1,000 women, 68% said they had not been given the opportunity by their employer to retrain or transition into digital roles.

"When the country is desperate for economic growth, we need to use whatever resource we have, and the resource of women who are mid-career, mid-experience. If they drop out of the market there are huge repercussions," Haines said.

The BBC understands that some London-based companies have stopped using AI tools for fear of bias in their recruitment.

Laura Holden, an AI lawyer and founder of the Bonsai AI and legal consultancy, said companies often do not understand how the tools work, which has the potential to cause "significant harm".

She argued it is difficult to determine whether there is bias because "there is a lack of regulation globally that requires providers to show how their tools work".

She pointed to CV screening tools and AI-scored interviews as examples of where bias can emerge.

One tool, she said, grades CVs from A to D, encouraging recruiters to prioritise higher-ranked candidates. Others flag factors such as a seven-year career gap as a "thing to note", potentially influencing decisions unfairly.

Holden said providers were "very quick" to claim their tools are safe and reduce bias, while designing and marketing them in ways that encourage employers to reject large numbers of applicants based on AI-generated scores. Although companies describe them as decision-support tools, she said they often functioned as "automated decision-making systems".

She called for mandatory testing and stronger regulation before AI recruitment tools are deployed, arguing existing laws were not designed with AI in mind.

Dr Eleanor Drage, a senior researcher at the University of Cambridge, said concerns about AI disadvantaging women in recruitment are "very justified".

She argued that human recruiters were better able to recognise the value of candidates returning from career breaks, such as maternity leave, and the transferable skills they bring - qualities AI may overlook.

While Drage said it was "very difficult" to prove AI recruitment tools are inherently biased, she argued the logic they operate by is "completely faulty" because they cannot assess a person's intrinsic value or personality in the way a human recruiter could.

She added that many recruiters do not fully understand how these tools work, and said companies should use AI to evaluate their own hiring practices rather than to assess "vulnerable populations, like older women going back into the workforce, or people who've had a career break".

While Drage acknowledges the benefits of using the tools, including helping hiring managers identify candidates with similar characteristics to people who have previously been hired, she says often "they're not on the side of the jobseeker".

The concerns raised in this article by interviewees relate to the use of AI-powered recruitment tools more broadly and are not directed at any single provider.

Workday, the maker of popular AI-powered human resources software, is facing claims that it violated Californian law thousands of times by ​weeding out job applicants at many major companies for discriminatory reasons.

The case is proceeding, with a ruling expected later this year.

The BBC contacted Workday, which said the claims in the suit were false, adding that its tools don't make hiring decisions.

More generally, Workday highlights that its recruitment tools help recruiters identify candidates who best match a job description based on their skills and experience, supporting rather than replacing human judgement.

The company said its AI was "rigorously tested" through its Responsible AI programme and "does not consider traits such as age or gender".

Workday added that, when used responsibly, AI can help qualified candidates avoid "getting lost in the pile".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently raised concerns about AI used in hiring, and that it hadn't made "recruitment fairer".

A government spokesperson said: "While AI can help employers manage large volumes of applications and reduce administrative burdens, it is vital that recruitment processes remain fair, transparent and accessible.

"Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed."

A spokesperson for Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said AI presented both opportunities and challenges, particularly as women are more likely to work in AI-exposed roles. They said the mayor had backed recommendations from the London AI and Jobs Taskforce to help employers adopt AI responsibly and support workers through the transition.

As for Stacey, she has set up a community chat and platform to help women feel less alone, and to help companies address the issues in question.

"I want us, as a group, to be heard and seen. And for gendered ageism to become a thing of the past.

"Because if we're lucky, we all get old."

Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook , X and Instagram . Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk

headline: An Indian cash scheme for women drops nine million beneficiaries - 29,000 were men
body:
Until two years ago, Nirmala Bawaskar had no bank account of her own.

A widow who works as a housemaid in Maharashtra's Sambhajinagar district, she signed documents with a thumbprint and had little control over money entering her household.

That changed when she enrolled in the Mukhyamantri Majhi Ladki Bahin Yojana, one of India's biggest state cash-transfer schemes. Launched just months before the state's closely fought election in 2024, it pays eligible women 1,500 rupees ($17; £13) a month and became both a financial lifeline for millions and one of the state's most potent political symbols.

For Bawaskar, the modest monthly payment meant her first bank account and money she could call her own.

"Though it is a small amount, it really helped us, especially with medical expenses," she says. "I was so motivated by it that I even learned how to write."

Bawaskar is one of more than 26 million women enrolled in the scheme, which is now under scrutiny over its implementation.

Last month, India's national auditor said Maharashtra's Women and Child Development Department overspent its authorised budget by 35.41bn rupees, spending a total of 332.37bn rupees on Ladki Bahin in its first financial year.

Separately, a government verification drive removed more than nine million beneficiaries – mostly for failing to complete mandatory identity checks, while others were found to be ineligible.

The Maharashtra government has not responded publicly to the audit. Women and Child Development Minister Aditi Tatkare's office told the BBC that a verification drive and recovery of ineligible payments were continuing but did not address the auditor's findings.

When Maharashtra launched Ladki Bahin in June 2024, it said the monthly payments would boost women's financial independence and help families meet their everyday expenses. The scheme covered eligible women aged 21 to 65 from lower-income households, excluding income-tax payers, government employees and families already receiving similar welfare benefits.

Its timing was politically significant. Announced after the ruling Mahayuti alliance – led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and two regional allies – suffered setbacks in India's 2024 general election, Ladki Bahin became the defining issue of the state election five months later. The government cast it as recognition of women's unpaid work, while the opposition called it vote-buying even as it promised similar cash transfers of its own.

When Mahayuti returned to power with a much larger-than-expected majority, its leaders credited Ladki Bahin with helping secure the victory.

A post-election survey by Lokniti-CSDS suggested the scheme helped Mahayuti. Half the women surveyed voted for the ruling alliance, compared with a third for the opposition. Among Ladki Bahin beneficiaries, Mahayuti's support rose to 54%.

But researchers cautioned against overstating its impact. Women were only three percentage points more likely than men to back Mahayuti, making it too early to conclude they had emerged as a distinct bloc of welfare voters, wrote CSDS researcher Rajeshwari Deshpande.

Maharashtra is not alone. Across India, governments led by different political parties have rolled out cash-transfer schemes for women, who now make up nearly half the country's electorate. The appeal is obvious: unlike roads or hospitals, the money arrives every month in a woman's own bank account – immediate, visible and personal.

But that popularity can also create pressure to launch schemes quickly and enrol millions of people. The auditor's report offered a glimpse of the risks.

Beyond the unauthorised spending, the auditor criticised the government for transferring 155.86bn rupees into special accounts in the final three months of the last financial year, despite no immediate need. It said the practice weakened financial discipline and reduced legislative oversight of public spending.

The verification drive exposed a different problem. Tatkare said the number of beneficiaries fell from 26.3 million to about 17 million after the government made electronic identity verification (e-KYC) mandatory.

Records obtained by The Indian Express under India's Right to Information law showed about 6.2 million of those removed – roughly two-thirds – had simply not completed e-KYC. When asked about this, Tatkare told BBC Marathi this should not be seen as evidence of fraud.

Others were excluded because they exceeded the income or age limits, belonged to families with government employees, were already receiving money through another welfare scheme or came from households where more than one person was claiming the benefit.

Government data also showed nearly 29,000 men and about 8,000 government employees had received payments. Tatkare said the state was recovering this money but did not say how much had been repaid.

The scrutiny has renewed questions about the benefits – and long-term costs – of cash-transfer programmes.

Neeraj Hatekar, a welfare economist, says Ladki Bahin has made a real difference to women with low and irregular incomes.

Drawing on labour-force data, he says women in Maharashtra earn about 300 rupees a day on average. Even if they get work for 20 days a month, they earn only 6,000-7,000 rupees. Against that, he says, the scheme's 1,500-rupee monthly payment "is a big amount".

But he argues the same needs could be addressed by investing more in stronger public services such as healthcare, education, childcare centres and transport, so that women do not have to spend as much on them.

Economist Ajit Ranade says governments must also weigh the fiscal costs. "You might divert funds to these schemes and win an election," he says. "But what about the long-term damage [to the state's finances]? That is never audited."

The audit may shape how the scheme is run in future. For women like Bawaskar, however, the Ladki Bahin scheme has already changed their lives.

The money has not lifted her family out of poverty. But it has given her something she never had before: money deposited into an account in her own name.

"It's money of my own," she says. "That's what matters to me."

headline: Australia PM under fire for remarks on Japanese counterpart's melon gifts
body:
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult.

During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good".

That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue.

Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands.

While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson."

"She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded.

The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia.

"The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday.

Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188).

"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.

During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China.

An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question".

He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights."

Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology.

Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting".

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said".

"I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven.

Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan.

The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above".

Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments".

Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

headline: US inflation eases as food and fuel costs cool
body:
US prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, slightly lower than the 3.5% in the year to June, new figures show.

Energy remained volatile as the Middle East conflict has continued. While gasoline prices were down 2.9% in July compared to June, they were up 24.6% over the year.

Month to month, inflation rose 0.1%, mainly due to an increase in housing costs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Even small moves in rent can lift the overall headline figure as it makes up a large share of household spending.

Food prices rose only slightly in July and at a slower rate than in June, while energy prices fell, offering some relief for consumers.

While inflation was slightly lower in July compared to June, that means prices are rising at a slower pace, not that prices overall are falling.

Prices excluding food and energy rose 0.2% after staying flat in June, with medical care and airline tickets edging higher and car insurance continuing to fall.

The new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, has said the central bank's priority is to "keep inflation moving down" while avoiding unnecessary shocks to the economy.

In a recent press briefing, Warsh said the Fed cannot use a "magic wand" to undo years of above-target inflation and must stay patient as price growth cools gradually.

One of the Fed's key jobs is to keep inflation near 2%, a level policymakers say keeps prices stable, supports steady economic growth, and helps prevent deeper downturns.

President Donald Trump has also said inflation is still too high for many families, pointing to rent and grocery bills as signs that the cost of living remains a major concern.

Financial markets reacted calmly to the latest figures, with stocks little changed as the figures were broadly in line with market expectations.

Recent labour market concerns have also softened expectations for a rate increase, after July's report showed a loss of jobs .

headline: How can Andy Burnham stop PC Harper's killers being released early?
body:
Just three weeks after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham is already unpicking a key piece of legislation passed under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The Sentencing Act 2026 was designed to produce a semi-permanent solution to the prisons overcrowding crisis, by releasing large numbers of prisoners earlier than had been previously planned.

After ordering a review, Burnham announced that he would exclude most rapists, child sex offenders and members of grooming gangs from the legislation.

But that left many people convicted of manslaughter still eligible for early release, including two of the men convicted of the manslaughter of PC Andrew Harper - prompting outcry from his family and former colleagues.

Burnham now says he is "increasingly confident" of being able to prevent the early release of "other serious offenders" including PC Harper's killers.

But how might he do that and why have the options he is looking at been previously rejected?

The prison population in England and Wales on 10 August was 86,536, which was 97% of the total capacity.

For decades politicians have been encouraging longer and longer sentences, but have not built the prisons to match.

If the prisons get completely full, courts will not be able to sentence murderers, rapists and other violent offenders. People suspected of the worst crimes will also have to be released instead of being held in custody ahead of their trials.

The controversial Sentencing Act 2026 made a number of key changes designed to see fewer people sent to prison, and to release many prisoners earlier than planned.

Following intense public and political pressure, Burnham now says he wants "a more focused approach" that will free up more prison spaces.

With the prisons in crisis, and no obvious way just to pick and choose who is released early, how can he do it?

In social media posts by the prime minister and his Justice Secretary Alex Norris, three areas were highlighted - female prisoners, foreign prisoners, and prisoners given the discredited Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences (IPPs) .

In England and Wales, 4% of prisoners are women. Generally, they have been convicted of less violent crimes than male prisoners, and are often victims of domestic abuse, or have substance abuse problems.

In theory, more than 2,000 women in prison for non-violent crimes could be released.

The former Prisons Minister Lord Timpson had long argued that there could be far fewer female prisoners. If one of the 12 prisons that hold women could be closed and reopened as a male prison, that would produce more headroom in the prison system.

This sounds like an easy fix, but reducing the number of women's prisons will mean some female inmates being held even further away from their families, and half of them are mothers, government data shows.

Women's prisons are also less secure than male prisons, so converting them would not be a quick or simple task.

Around 12% of the prison population, more than 10,000 people, are foreign nationals - though only around 6,500 are eligible for deportation, government data shows, as the rest are awaiting trial or sentencing.

One way of reducing the number of prisoners in England and Wales would be to deport the foreign nationals, long before they have completed their sentences. The Sentencing Act actually has a clause, not yet enacted, that would allow foreign nationals to be deported at the point of sentence.

But deporting prisoners convicted of violent crimes and sex offences before they have served a substantial part of their sentences could be politically unpalatable, so this will need to be considered carefully.

There are also huge problems with deporting foreign prisoners. In many cases foreign offenders who have even completed their sentences end up being released into the community in the UK instead of being deported, because of logistical problems, including the difficulty in getting travel documents from some countries.

In theory this is the area with the most potential, but beneath the simple number - more than 10,000 (which is in fact around 6,500) - lurk some tricky problems that need working through.

Another apparently easy option is the controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, known as IPPs.

These IPP sentences were introduced for prisoners convicted of serious sexual or violent offences by Lord Blunkett when he was home secretary, and he has long since disowned them.

They came into force in 2005 and ran until they were abolished in 2012.

Prisoners sentenced to IPPs were told they would not be released until it was safe to do so, but they have found it hard to show that they are no longer a risk and many have languished in prison for years and years.

According to Ministry of Justice data, 2,271 people are serving IPP sentences as of June. Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so.

As all IPP prisoners have been inside since at least 2012, it would be easy just to say they should all be released. But that carries huge risks.

While there are likely to be some reformed characters in the 2,271, at least some of them will be people who are still extremely dangerous. Quite possibly much more dangerous than PC Harper's killers.

What Burnham is trying to do is free up a few hundred more prison spaces so that he could exclude another category of prisoners from early release - one that would include PC Harper's killers.

That could be for example, everyone convicted of manslaughter who is serving a determinate sentence - informally estimated as just under 500 people.

That could be further reduced by excluding only those convicted of manslaughter who had been given a determinate sentence of more than 10 years, as an example.

Just focusing on people convicted of the manslaughter of emergency workers would probably not work, as that was not a specific offence category until recently.

If the prime minister managed to find a category that did not exclude too many prisoners from early release, but did keep PC Harper's killers inside then he would satisfy the campaign and the petition which now has more than 900,000 signatures.

But none of the possible solutions he has proposed today are quick or easy. They are intractable problems that have not previously been solved. What is more, some of them also carry political risk.

Sometimes a fresh set of eyes can identify innovative solutions that have been previously missed. Sometimes they just discover that there are no easy solutions.

headline: Tata Group Chairman N Chandrasekaran to step down in February
body:
N Chandrasekaran, the chairman of Tata Group, has said that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.

The 63-year-old said the decision came after the board of Tata Sons could not reach a resolution on a five-year extension of his term, months after the proposal first came up.

The news sent shares of listed Tata companies plunging and has led to questions over what lies ahead for the gigantic salt-to-steel conglomerate that owns Air India, Tata Steel and Jaguar Land Rover.

Chandrasekaran's resignation, which comes days ahead of Tata Sons' annual general meeting, points to tensions that have been playing out for months after a boardroom power battle erupted between trustees.

The Tata Group is uniquely structured - a charitable arm called Tata Trusts owns 66% of the group's parent company, Tata Sons. This has given the group tax and regulatory advantages, and allows it to carry out charitable activities, but experts say that its dual non-profit and commercial objectives have sometimes led to governance issues.

Tata Trusts has three nominees on the Tata Sons board. Reports have said that the board members have disagreed over issues such as board nominations, funding approvals and the public listing of Tata Sons. The group has not publicly commented on the discord.

The internal rifts threatened to distract the group while it was facing severe business headwinds including the revival of Air India , which it bought from the Indian government in 2022.

When the proposal for his extension was brought before the board in February, one board member did not support it, Chandrasekaran said in his statement without naming the person.

"In the absence of unanimous support, I chose to defer the decision," he said, adding that there was no resolution even six months later.

"Tata Sons is a very large institution and there are many strategic projects that are under critical stages of execution. It is not only necessary to have a leader in place to lead the Group beyond Feb 2027, but also clarity on leadership is important for employees, investors, partners and other stakeholders," he said.

Chandrasekaran was named the group's chairman in 2017. He replaced the late Cyrus Mistry, whose abrupt removal from the post months earlier had triggered a bitter legal battle.

Before becoming chairman, Chandrasekaran was the CEO and managing director of the group's high-profile global IT service provider, Tata Consultancy Services. He joined the group in 1987 - a 2017 press release announcing his appointment as chairman described him as a "Tata lifer".

Ambareesh Baliga, an independent market analyst, said that when a person with Chandrasekaran's stature stepped down like this, it was inevitable that the markets would react negatively.

"However, they have six months to find a good successor," he said, adding that he thought it likely that the next leader would be chosen from within the group.

headline: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
body:
Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally.

In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.

The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea".

"The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world.

He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments.

It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea.

Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces.

Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024.

In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months.

In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military.

He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary".

Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs.

All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations.

One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires.

Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering.

Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko.

He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon.

Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages.

Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted.

It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors.

Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region.

Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated.

In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses.

Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.

The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery.

Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.

The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

headline: Poorest areas should not house all asylum seekers, says Burnham
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has suggested that wealthier areas of the UK should house more asylum seekers.

"We cannot have a situation where it's only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers," he told GB News on Tuesday.

His comments came in response to a question about protests which have taken place in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire over plans to provide accommodation for asylum seekers on a nearby former military base.

But shadow home secretary Chris Philp, responding to Burnham's comments, said: "We shouldn't be housing illegal immigrants anywhere – wealthy or not."

Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast on Wednesday morning, immigration minister Anna Turley said the number of hotels had gone from a peak of 400 under the Conservatives to 160 under Labour, and pledged all of them would close by 2029.

Turley said the government had already saved £1bn by closing hotels and opening alternative, secure sites for asylum seekers, including two former military bases, student accommodation and former industrial sites around the country.

"I think this is about fairness and we won't be asking anybody to take more than they can, and we won't be asking anyone to take more than their fair share," she said.

"What we've seen in the past is places like Blackpool, and other communities around the country where housing is perhaps cheaper and more plentiful, have had to take more than their fair share of asylum seekers," she added.

"That's put a huge burden on local communities and created real civil unrest, so we want to make sure that we're managing the system much better in a more sustained way that's reducing the impact on local communities.

"It's important that everybody plays their fair share in that, and it's about making sure that no one community is more over-pressured or overburdened than others."

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.

He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.

Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.

The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution .

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

headline: Man, 102, in critical condition after alleged pub assault
body:
A 102-year-old man is in a critical condition after allegedly being assaulted at a pub.

Emergency services were called to The Crow's Nest pub in Cwmbran, Torfaen, at about 22:25 BST on 1 August, and the man was taken to hospital.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, and has since been released under investigation.

Gwent Police is appealing for witnesses and want to speak to anyone who was in the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 on the night of the incident.

headline: 'Not afraid to stay': The Canadians who want to change how wildfires are fought
body:
When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put.

He put sprinklers on his roof to extinguish falling embers. He checked on elders in his community who also stayed behind, and he fuelled up four boats down on the lake in case they needed a quick escape.

"This is everything I've built in my 58 years," Wigwas, a councillor from Gull Bay First Nation, told the BBC. "I'm just not going to run away and let it burn."

Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023, when blazes tore through forest land roughly the size of Syria. As of this August, more than 750 wildfires are actively burning across the country.

The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities. Even President Donald Trump has taken note, threatening to further tariff Canada for allowing "filthy, polluted" air to waft south of the border.

The intensifying wildfires have sparked a national conversation: Are there enough firefighters to battle these more challenging fire seasons? What happens when resources are stretched too thin? And how can remote communities, often closest to danger because of their proximity to Canada's vast boreal forest, learn to live with this new reality?

Wigwas asked himself these questions when he decided to stay, even as he faces a fine of around C$800 ($570; £425) for defying evacuation orders.

Leaders of Gull Bay First Nation, also known as Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek, have been urging residents to stay away since mid-July as more than 150 wildfires burn across Ontario's northwest.

Its chief penned a letter on 29 July pleading with those who have remained to leave immediately, saying that Ontario firefighters cannot do their jobs safely with people still in their homes.

It is the same message officials across the country have been conveying in British Columbia, where around 115 fires are currently burning.

But with a wildfire 24km outside his community, Wigwas, speaking in late July, said he had yet to see fire personnel from out of town there to help fireproof properties or keep an eye out on the elders who remained.

He said it made him realise that his First Nation would benefit from setting up its own wildfire emergency response and teaching residents how to protect their own homes.

"Everybody talks about climate change, but nobody is doing something to unite the (First Nations) reserves and have a system like that set up," Wigwas said.

Dave Bradley, a spokesperson for Ontario's ministry of natural resources, did not address Wigwas' claim directly, but said the province has been in "constant contact" with First Nations leaders.

He added that fire fighting resources are directed based on "fire behaviour, weather conditions and risks to communities."

In the west-coast province of British Columbia - long the front line of Canada's wildfire response - people are doing just what Wigwas is envisioning for his First Nation, with efforts underway to train residents of rural and remote communities how to safely respond to wildfires before out-of-town crews can arrive.

Sonja Leverkus, a wildfire researcher and specialist, said she has helped train more than 400 people in and around her community of Fort Nelson over the last three years through a firefighting group she helped start called the Northeast BC Rural Incident Management Team.

She told the BBC that her efforts are inspired by a realisation that Canada needs to change how it fights wildfires as climate change increases their frequency and intensity.

"There are not enough human beings in Canada," she said, with the appropriate training, "to fight the fires that we have currently, especially over the last five years".

Remote communities, where the nearest town might be hundreds of kilometres away, can sometimes be bumped down the priority list for BC firefighting crews if there are blazes threatening more populated areas, she said.

Her crew, who are primarily indigenous, have carried out prescribed burns, also known as a hazard reduction burns – a practice of setting planned, controlled blazes to remove fuels that could contribute to wildfires.

They have also helped put out smaller fires before they grow out of control using fire wagons that they purchased through fundraising and grants, sometimes arriving ahead of provincial firecrews and then working in tandem with them, Leverkus said.

When a major wildfire tore through Fort Nelson in 2024, she said she and 40 of her team members stayed behind and were hired by the province to clear flammables and support fire suppression activities.

Leverkus also organised a structural protection training course for locals to learn how to shield buildings from embers that can quickly spur fires that engulf entire towns.

"We have mechanics, we have carpenters, we have real good problem solvers," Leverkus said. "We're all not afraid to stay."

Cam Allen, a 70-year-old former helicopter pilot in Fort Nelson who has previously fought fires from the air, said he recently took Leverkus' course to learn about ground fire suppression techniques, and, more broadly, how to help if a blaze reaches his town.

He mentioned John Carr, a California man who went viral last year for staying behind and warding off flames with a garden hose during the Palisades fire, ultimately saving his home even when others around it burned down.

"It makes you wonder, if 100 people had stayed or 1,000 people had stayed behind and actually did what he did, how much more could have been saved?" Allen asked.

But not all were as fortunate as Carr during the Los Angeles fires, which killed a total of 29 people – a few of whom had, too, defied evacuation orders in order to protect their homes, even as officials urged thousands in the area to leave.

Leverkus' group is not officially recognised by BC's government, and what it is trying to achieve highlights simmering tensions in fire-prone regions between those who enforce evacuation orders and those who defy them.

Last week, wildfire crews in BC were forced to rescue a man when his home in the Village of Clinton was surrounded by flames, after he had refused to evacuate.

In a wildfire update on Tuesday, BC's minister responsible for emergency management reiterated that all those who are under evacuation orders should leave.

"We may not be able to get back to you if an emergency happens," warned Minister Kelly Greene, adding that evacuation orders are made as "a last resort to keep people and communities safe".

Paul Kovacs, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario and director of its Catastrophic Loss Reduction Institute, said that Canada has had a lower fatality rate from wildfires despite their frequency in part because of its evacuation approach.

The stay and defend mindset, he said, "is aggressively opposed" by the academic community in Canada, as opposed to other fire-prone countries like Australia.

"In the hierarchy of what is it that you do to manage a wildfire, preservation of life is first," Kovacs said.

Rural and remote communities can and should play an outsized role in informing officials of how best to protect their town, he said, and can do a lot of work to fire proof homes and structures. But that work, he argued, should not be done "while the fire is burning."

A spokesperson for BC's Ministry of Forests told the BBC that self-organised groups in rural areas can be hired temporarily by the province during an active wildfire, but only when there are no more available provincial firefighters in the area.

The ministry added that BC Wildfire's full-time staff has increased by 56% in recent years to respond to the growing frequency of fires, in addition to seasonal staff.

Leverkus said she has been exploring ways to have her programme recognised by BC officials so that those trained through it can also help without being penalised for staying behind.

She added that safety precautions are engrained in her courses, including training on how to predict fire behaviour and mapping out at least two safe escape routes.

Not all of those who are trained want to stay back, she said, but those that do receive orders from trained crew commanders, including on when it's time to leave.

"If people want to stay and defend, they need to understand what that means for themselves, what that means for their family," Leverkus said.

Her goal is for the programme to one day become a blueprint that can be adopted by rural and remote communities across Canada, creating teams that can be relied on across the country.

As for Wigwas, he will be fighting his evacuation fine in court.

"If the chief and council want to charge me for saving my house, and I end up with nowhere to live, I might as well be in jail," he said.

headline: Rod Stewart calls off US tour after 'routine' heart procedure
body:
Sir Rod Stewart has called off the remaining dates of his US tour after having what was described as a "routine" heart procedure.

The 81-year-old singer has been advised by doctors to recuperate for the next four weeks following a coronary stent procedure.

A stent is a small wire tube that can be inserted into coronary arteries, which supply blood to the heart, if they have become narrowed or blocked.

"I'm already feeling better and very much on the mend," Sir Rod said on Instagram .

"I want to thank the doctors, nurses and everyone who has taken such wonderful care of me.

"I am deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon."

The veteran singer, known for classic hits like Maggie May, Sailing and Do Ya Think I'm Sexy?, had been due to perform 11 concerts in the US in the coming weeks, including a six-date residency in Las Vegas.

He had already cancelled shows in Cincinnati on Sunday and Cleveland on Tuesday because of what was described as "an unforeseen but minor medical procedure".

A new statement posted on Instagram on Tuesday said: "Following further medical evaluation, Sir Rod Stewart has successfully undergone a routine coronary stent procedure.

"Doctors are pleased with his recovery, and Rod is doing very well and has returned to his normal daily activities. On the advice of his doctors, he will take the next four weeks to recuperate and regain full fitness before returning to the stage.

"Unfortunately, this means he will be unable to continue his current tour dates.

"Information regarding affected performances will be communicated by the respective promoters and venues."

Sir Rod also has three dates in his tour schedule for Mexico in September, for which tickets are currently still on sale.

headline: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketer
body:
"You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?"

Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi.

Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me."

Years later, that prediction has come true.

On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August.

For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment.

Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor.

"There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says.

But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind.

"After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him."

Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible.

"Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this? There's no future in it.' We came from a place where there was no concept of playing sport professionally and hardly any infrastructure."

To pursue his dream, Auqib regularly travelled around 70km (43 miles) to Srinagar to practise on proper cricket pitches. He did not even own a pair of spike shoes when he attended his first cricket trials.

But his work ethic never changed, his cousin Bilal says.

"Auqib is very hardworking and consistent. He knows how to fight obstacles and make a way for himself.

"He would wake up early to go to the gym and then practise for the rest of the day. He did that almost every day for 10 years."

His breakthrough came in 2020 when he made his Ranji Trophy (India's top domestic tournament) debut for Jammu and Kashmir, taking a five-wicket haul against Jharkhand.

Former India all-rounder Parvez Rasool, Jammu and Kashmir's first international cricketer and Auqib's long-time captain, says one quality always stood out.

"I have followed Auqib's progress for a long time, and what stands out about him is his work ethic and discipline."

Success, however, did not come overnight. Auqib claimed 44 wickets during the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, finishing as the competition's leading fast bowler, but remained largely outside the national conversation.

"When you do well but don't get recognition, it hurts," his father says.

"But we should never lose hope. Hope is what keeps the world intact. I always believed his time would come."

It did.

The following season, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matches to finish as the tournament's leading wicket-taker and help Jammu and Kashmir win their maiden Ranji Trophy title after a wait of 67 years.

Those performances earned him an 84m rupees (£730,000; $982,000) Indian Premier League (IPL) contract with Delhi Capitals. Although opportunities in the IPL were limited, his red-ball exploits had already caught the attention of India's selectors.

For Rasool, Auqib's Test call-up carries significance far beyond one player.

"Playing Test cricket is the ultimate dream for any cricketer. It was my dream too. Seeing Auqib earn that call-up fills me with immense pride.

"In a way, it feels like a dream many of us in Jammu and Kashmir carried has finally been realised through him. It is a historic moment not just for Auqib and his family, but for cricket across the region."

He believes Auqib's journey is remarkable not just because he reached the Indian team, but because of where he came from.

"Making it to the Indian team is incredibly difficult for any player, but the challenge is even greater when you come from Jammu and Kashmir. For years, we have had limited infrastructure, fewer opportunities and many obstacles that players from other parts of the country don't necessarily face.

"To reach this level, you need exceptional consistency, mental strength and the determination to keep believing in yourself. Auqib has shown all of those qualities, which is why this achievement is so special."

Jammu and Kashmir became affiliated with the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) in 1957, yet the region still has only two major cricket stadiums, both with limited facilities. Long winters, heavy snowfall and decades of conflict have further slowed cricket's development.

"This is a landmark moment for cricket in Jammu and Kashmir," Rasool says.

"For a long time, people questioned whether someone from our region could make it to India's Test team. Auqib has answered that question. His selection shows players from Jammu and Kashmir can compete with the best if they are given the opportunity."

He believes Auqib's journey will inspire a new generation.

"When I started playing, there weren't many role models from Jammu and Kashmir. Today, things are changing.

"Auqib becoming the first player from the region to earn an India Test call-up will give countless youngsters the belief that they can dream big too. His journey proves that no matter where you come from or what challenges you face, hard work and perseverance can take you to the highest level."

Back in Baramulla, Ghulam Nabi now finds himself recognised everywhere he goes.

"People come up to me, hug me and say, 'This is Auqib's father.'

"It makes me immensely proud."

headline: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
body:
Do you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?

The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.

But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.

Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago.

But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?

When the BBC spoke to shoppers in central London this week, the retailer seemed to divide opinion.

Some, like Enrico, 28, said they loved the convenience of same-day collection, and felt nostalgic towards a brand which unlocked fond childhood memories.

"It was a great way of doing your Christmas shopping," he told the BBC. "We'd go into our local Argos and we'd get the massive print catalogue."

Argos's encyclopedia-like catalogue was once dubbed "the laminated book of dreams", but the company stopped printing it in 2021 .

At one point it was Europe's most widely printed publication.

For others, though, Argos has not moved with the times and is at odds with the seemingly endless online choice.

"I feel Amazon is a lot easier because it gets delivered straight to your door with Prime," said Emily, 22, adding that she only used Argos to buy appliances, not "day to day" items.

Jack Cunningham, 26, from Kent often uses Argos to pick up things when he's at work in London.

The scientist said the big draw was convenience: "If I need something in the moment and can't wait for delivery, normally I'll get it in Argos.

"You can order something really cheap on Amazon, and it might come and be the wrong size, " he added.

For years, commentators have asked whether Argos could build a business to take on Amazon, the biggest online seller in the UK.

But while Argos has invested a lot in digital, it never quite happened. It made £4.1bn of sales last year, compared with £32bn for Amazon in the UK.

Argos does, however, offer something its online rivals don't - a large network of stores, concessions in Sainsbury's shops, and collection points that mean customers can click and collect on the same day, free of charge.

Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth thinks Argos could capitalise on this, along with its reputation as a trusted British brand.

However, she thinks it needs to improve its app so it can compete with online players like Amazon, Shein and Temu.

"I think if you asked people to name five High Street retailers, they wouldn't name Argos," she added. "It's almost about reminding people it exists."

Argos hasn't been front of mind for Georgia, 27, for ages. She thinks it is outdated and not for her. "It's very old school isn't it? I'm more of an Amazon shopper."

Argos could also do better on customer service, thinks Hugh Radojev, editor of Retail Week.

"It's not an exciting place to shop, or what it used to be for kids around Christmas. Under a new ownership you'd hope they could get it back into the zeitgeist."

Since 2012, Argos has gone from having 845 standalone shops to around 200 - although it also has opened about 450 shop-within-shops in Sainsbury's stores.

This was seen as a smart move, allowing Argos to tap into Sainsbury's large customer base. Argos will keep all of those concessions after the takeover, and customers will continue to get Nectar loyalty card points for all their purchases.

But Nicole, 40, an Argos fan from South London, says she wants the chain to expand further.

"It would be nice if they could go in other supermarkets like Tesco," she added.

Argos's new owners have ruled out deals with rival supermarkets, but they do plan to forge other "partnerships" and open new standalone stores.

The group, called Swift Partners, includes several seasoned retail veterans, one of them a former boss of Co-operative Group. Retail analyst Richard Hyman thinks this ownership will be a better fit than Sainsbury's, which was focused on selling food.

But he is sceptical about how much Argos can grow in such a "tough retail market".

Shuttleworth is more optimistic, saying with a "ruthless focus" Argos can thrive and even put Amazon under pressure.

"Argos completely revolutionised the way we shop when they came out and they have a history of being different," she said. "If I was marketing director I would be thinking about how to bottle that for 2027."
