headline: EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US firm
body:
No-frills airline EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a £5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo after a rival bidder dropped out.

The takeover was agreed after US investment firm Castlelake, which had made a series of offers for the carrier, said it was withdrawing from the bid battle.

Apollo said it wants to help the airline grow and that it does not intend to cut any jobs in the first 12 months after the takeover has been completed, implying that passengers can expect largely the same service.

EasyJet is one of Europe's largest airlines. It employs more than 19,000 people, and flies around 1,200 routes across 35 European countries.

It was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer cheap air fares to Europe from the UK. Its first flights took off in November 1995 flying from Luton to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with its first international flights the following year.

Sir Stelios and his family still own around 15% of the business, and he said he supported Apollo's plans for the airline "to create more growth".

"My family and I intend to remain invested as long-term major shareholders of EasyJet for the next chapter in the company's journey," he said in a statement.

The future ownership of EasyJet has been uncertain since it emerged in late May that Castlelake was considering a bid for the airline.

Castlelake made a number of approaches for EasyJet, which were rebuffed initially after the carrier accused the US firm of trying to buy it "on the cheap".

In early July, EasyJet and Castlelake said they had agreed a deal in principle , but then Apollo - which owns Wagamama parent The Restaurant Group - swooped in with a higher bid.

Under the offer from Apollo, EasyJet shareholders will receive £7.15 per share.

AJ Bell's head of financial analysis, Danni Hewson said while the offer was significantly above where the company's shares were trading before the Iran war, the figure was "still woefully short of the company's pre-pandemic highs".

Apollo said it was "highly supportive" of the airline's existing strategy, adding there was "a significant opportunity to accelerate the operational and commercial ambitions" for the EasyJet Group.

"EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand," said Alex van Hoek, partner and European private equity lead at Apollo.

EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said "We welcome Apollo's commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for EasyJet."

The deal will still need to win approval from regulators, including in the EU where rules mean EasyJet's owners will have to be majority EU-based.

Apollo anticipates this can be achieved by making the Haji-Ioannou family, and other EU-based shareholders, owners of around half of the business.

Apollo said though it does not intend to cut any staff for at least 12 months after the deal goes through, if the deal completes and EasyJet delists from the stock exchange to become a private company, some jobs related to maintaining its public-listed operations could go.

The firm said that would be a "limited number of roles in specific areas."

AJ Bell's Hewson said the potential loss of another well-known name from London markets will be seen as a blow.

"Air travel might not be as sexy as space travel, but retail investors understand it and names like EasyJet can't easily be replaced," she said.

headline: German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
body:
As Germany investigates how a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway at Leipzig airport, there is renewed talk in Europe of hybrid war.

The interior minister is warning of a "new level of danger" from an attack that "may involve foreign powers".

There is no proof at this stage to link the flying bomb directly to Russia, which denies any role. But as well as the means and the motive, Moscow does have form.

The BBC has seen details of the investigation into a plot in 2024 in which Russian-linked proxies in Poland and Lithuania not only handled drones and explosives but also delivered them to Germany.

The quadcopter was discovered at Leipzig airport late on Tuesday night, forcing one runway into lockdown as a bomb disposal robot rolled into action.

On the tarmac close by were several Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes, stripes along their enormous bodies in the blue and yellow of the country's flag. One reads, "Be Brave Like Kherson", the southern city now on the frontline of Russia's invasion.

Pictures published by German media suggest the drone was a relatively small device which airport staff spotted "floating" between the Ukrainian planes.

Around the same time, a DHL cargo plane collided with an "unidentified object" as it pulled up into the sky, unable to land in Leipzig.

Teams are still working to establish whether that was a second drone.

They are also trying to trace who launched the devices and why.

A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.

In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage.

A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence.

But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before.

Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT.

"Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added.

The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets.

The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb.

Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found.

While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential.

One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior".

He has since pleaded not guilty in court.

One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain.

He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside.

He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road.

For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape.

"Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators.

These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up.

Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside.

The intended targets were never revealed.

In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear.

And what about the Leipzig case?

Few details about the drone bomb are yet public.

Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery.

We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited.

"The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained.

But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear.

Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe.

Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid.

"It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained.

"You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious."

And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly".

"We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC.

Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response.

The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine.

Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there."

But Russia watchers are clear.

"This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities."

He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war.

"My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment."

headline: Estonia rejects proposals to take prisoners from UK jails
body:
The Estonian government has rejected the idea of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British jails.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a deal signed last week.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.

The Labour government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Pakosta said Estonia had received no proposals to rent its prison space from the UK, adding that if one was to be made "our answer would be unequivocal - in Margaret Thatcher's famous words: No. No. No."

She added: "Such a proposal would not merely be mistaken, misguided or unacceptable; it would deserve to be rejected outright."

Thatcher memorably repeated "no" three times in 1990 speech, as she fiercely rejected calls for deeper political and economic integration of the European Community, which later evolved into the European Union.

In 2024, the Labour government, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, held talks with Estonia to discuss the Baltic state's policy to house some prisoners from abroad.

Pakosta previously told the BBC she had met then-UK Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood in Lithuania.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is planning to release thousands of prisoners early this October, as it scrambles to free up space in jails almost at 100% capacity.

On Monday, Downing Street did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons, when asked by reporters if the government was considering doing so.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government was focused on "creating that extra capacity within the system domestically".

"In terms of renting prison places abroad, it's just not a quick fix," the spokesperson added.

"It will require primary legislation underpinned by a complex international agreement which would take several years to agree."

A government source told the BBC that renting foreign prison space would not help with the short-term crisis in jails.

Burnham has ordered the justice secretary to come up with a plan to create more space in jails by September.

He said the plan would be based on removing more foreign national offenders from prisons, releasing some offenders on indefinite sentences, and using space in women's jails for male inmates.

Other parties have come up with their own ideas for dealing with overcrowding in prisons.

At a news conference on Monday, Reform UK suggested 10,000 prison spaces could be freed up if all foreign criminals were sent abroad to serve their sentences.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said his party was exploring options to transfer foreign criminals in the UK to prisons in other countries, including El Salvador and Kosovo.

When asked if he had other countries in mind, Farage said: "Yes there are Baltic state options as well.

"I mean, conversations could certainly be had with Lithuania, for example, or perhaps Estonia as well."

A Reform UK spokesman said its policy was focused on El Salvador, Kosovo and "possibly others if they are open to the idea".

In recent days, the Conservatives have also urged Burnham to revive their plan to rent prison cells overseas, a policy they introduced when the party was in government in 2023.

The proposal aimed to mirror models used by Norway and Belgium in the Netherlands, where both countries rented cells to deal with overcrowding in their prisons.

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said this was "an idea that we legislated for in government but Labour subsequently did not pursue that".

"That was a catastrophic mistake by the Labour government that should be urgently reversed."

The Conservatives did not respond to requests to comment on Estonia's rejection of a prison rental deal with the UK.

In a statement, Lithuania's Ministry of Justice said: "There have been no discussions or consultations regarding the possibility of accepting the transfer of all Lithuanian citizens imprisoned in the United Kingdom".

A spokesperson said the Lithuanian government did not "see any scope for entering into practical arrangements of this kind".

The Kosovo government, which has agreed to lease 300 of its jail cells to Denmark as part of a deal worth £170m (€200m), appeared more open to working with other countries on prisoner transfers.

A Kosovo government spokesperson said: "We value the willingness of partner countries to initiate and advance new co-operation initiatives that serve common interests, mutual priorities, and the strengthening of international justice mechanisms".

But the spokesperson stressed Kosovo would focus on enacting its deal with Denmark "before entering into any new agreement of a similar nature".

The BBC has previously been told both former Conservative and Labour ministers independently came to the view that renting prison space abroad would be expensive.

Sweden has agreed to pay up to £52m (€61m) a year to Estonia if the Baltic nation does house 600 of its offenders at the Tartu prison.

Estonia said from the 301st inmate onwards, Sweden would pay an additional £7,254 (€8,500) per prisoner, per month.

The average annual cost per prisoner in a public-sector prison in England and Wales was £60,018 in 2024/25, according to Ministry of Justice data.

headline: Ban on 'subscription traps' brought forward by three months
body:
Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.

The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much higher prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers £400m a year in total, or up to £170 per person.

At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.

It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

It is already unlawful to use false "was" prices for items on sale, but it is not on the list of the Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) list of banned practices.

Practices on the list, such as operating pyramid schemes or displaying a quality assurance mark without authorisation, are automatically considered illegal without consumer harm having to be proved.

The Liberal Democrats urged Burnham to "go further" to protect consumers, with Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper calling for "strengthened protections against rogue traders" and action to tackle supermarket "shrinkflation" — the practice of products being made smaller yet being sold for the same price.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a £2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

Chris Fell, a photographer from Wiltshire, told BBC Your Voice he had to cancel his debit card in order to get out of a subscription trap.

The 71-year-old had signed up for Viewbug, a service he wanted to use to show off his pictures and build a portfolio.

But he complained the subscription costs "doubled" in the three years he was using the service, adding that "the renewal was going through automatically and they would not cancel it".

In order to break the subscription, Fell said: "I resorted to asking my bank to cancel a debit card so that a new card would be issued with a different 16 digit number.

"Job done and then I just waited for the US-based company to ask for a new debit card number which I then declined."

Viewbug's co-founder Ori Guttin said he was "sorry to hear about Chris's experience" and that it had struggled to help with his membership queries due to the use of multiple email addresses.

He said the company is small and "cares deeply about the photography community we've built", and while it does not "get everything right… we work hard to support our members and resolve issues when they arise".

For certain contracts such as broadband and mobile phones, you may have certain rights to cancel already, but it depends on the circumstances.

You may be legally entitled to cancel if there is a problem with the service provided, such as poor broadband speed.

headline: Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war
body:
"I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."

That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in February.

An Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders – and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years.

Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view.

"Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes.

These comments hint at the personal nature of this war – and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety.

Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy.

It was an elaborate ruse, which included the president being transported to and from aircraft inside a catering truck, in response to what American officials reportedly believed to be credible intelligence of an Iranian missile threat to Air Force One.

The White House has given little detail about this threat - but nonetheless it marks another striking episode in the turbulent history of Trump's relationship with Iran.

Government security experts have said such measures are not unusual when a president travels in or near a warzone.

Past presidents have travelled to places like Afghanistan, Iraq and Ukraine under cover of secrecy – but never without at least some prior knowledge by media outlets, under agreements that they would not disclose the movement until after the fact.

The optics of Trump hiding in a catering truck from an apparent Iranian threat are less than ideal for a president who has repeatedly touted his strength - as well as the frailty of Iran's military after months of war.

The secrecy in the days and weeks after the Secret Service operation in Ankara may have been, in part, to avoid undermining his public image of power.

The operation, which took more than a month to come to light, also underscores the apparent threat Iran continues to present to US interests in a conflict that the president asserts is all but wrapped up against an adversary he has said has been thoroughly defeated on the battlefield.

Iranian threats against Trump are not new, however.

After Trump, in his first term, ordered the January 2020 missile strike that killed Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) leader Qasem Soleimani, Iran's leaders promised reprisals against the American president and senior administration leaders.

In one instance, an Iranian mural depicted a drone targeting Trump while he played golf in Florida.

It appears that there were more to these Iranian threats than just posturing.

The Biden administration warned Iran in 2022 not to target any US citizens, after unearthing a plan to target former Trump National Security Adviser John Bolton.

And in July 2024, US law enforcement arrested a Pakistani man , Asif Merchant, who allegedly had ties to the IRGC, for plotting to kill Trump. Four months later, an Afghani citizen, Farhad Shakeri, was charged with another assassination scheme against Trump.

Merchant was convicted in March 2026, but Shakeri, who US prosecutors allege was directed by an IRGC official, is still at large.

Although these attempts were foiled during the planning stages, the physical risks Trump faced as he sought a return to the White House were all too apparent.

In July 2024 he was left bloodied after a gunman opened fire at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Two months later, an armed man was arrested in Florida after US Secret Service agents spotted him hiding in the trees near where Trump was playing golf.

"It was a galvanising moment for him," Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for the New York Times, said in a recent interview when discussing both the Iranian plots and assassination attempts of 2024. "All of that in his mind becomes one big blur."

"For Trump himself, Iran and this feeling of being under threat is constant," she said.

The president, according to the news website Semafor , often muses - and jokes - about becoming a target of assassination.

"Nobody told me how dangerous it is to be president, and if they had told me, I probably wouldn't have run," one White House official recounted Trump as saying. "And he makes comments like that in jest, but there's a reality behind that."

Trump's bombing of Iran's nuclear research facilities in 2025, and this year's expansive bombing campaign and naval blockade, prompted a new round of Iranian threats against Trump – and a direct warning by the US president in response.

In July, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had made threats "to assassinate, or attempt to assassinate" him and said 1,000 "missiles are Locked and Loaded and aimed at the Islamic Republic of Iran, with thousands more to immediately follow, should the Iranian Government act on its threat".

The president's message to Iran was blunt. Many of the recent threats against him have been unequivocal, too.

At the funeral service for Khamenei, held the day before Trump departed Turkey, participants carried a banner that read "#KillTrump". The following week, in a square in central Tehran, a building featured a large mural of the American president, lying in a black coffin, with the words "We will kill Trump" and "Blood for blood" written below it.

Iran has denied involvement in any previous plots against Trump, but the message – delivered after Khamenei's death and reports of Iranian civilian casualties in US and Israeli strikes – has been clear.

The war, Iranians are saying, is far from over. And Trump, himself, is a target for revenge.

On the final leg of the journey back to the US from Turkey, as Trump and his travelling media pool were reunited on the same aircraft, the president came back to the press cabin to talk to reporters.

They asked about the unusual journey, which included an order by the Secret Service that the window shades on the decoy plane be closed during takeoff from Ankara.

"I have read all the time I'm number one on their list," he told them.

"But if I go, you go, right?"

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

headline: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft
body:
Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother.

Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety.

"Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says.

An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts.

The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves.

By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it.

The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam.

The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps.

The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated.

For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound.

"This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says.

Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime.

Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km.

She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building.

Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'.

Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it.

She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed.

None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says.

The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly.

Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages.

About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp.

For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil.

Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats. Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill.

But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before?

Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley, a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms".

The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates.

As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251.

In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat.

Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology.

Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam.

"What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography.

For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal.

She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week.

Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have.

So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life.

She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance.

Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee?

"No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before."

"We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

headline: Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president
body:
Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state.

The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous.

His task will be to monitor Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace Orbán's constitution of 2011.

"We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," András Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6.

"The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs."

All 51 MPs belonging to Orbán's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, Tamás Sulyok, from the post last month .

In his speech, András Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution.

Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking Orbán's legacy.

Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution.

The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which Orbán used to govern by decree, were all cancelled.

The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government.

Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law.

Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July , as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs.

Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored.

If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening.

In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives.

Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

"I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking."

Baka was elected today as a transitional figure.

Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible, the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years.

Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders.

"The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people."

headline: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez
body:
Football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo has married his longtime partner, model and influencer Georgina Rodríguez, in a civil ceremony in Portugal.

The Portuguese striker posted an image on his Instagram account showing two hands, presumed to be his on top of his wife's, both wearing wedding rings.

Calling it the wedding of the year, Portuguese media say the couple tied the knot on 11 August in the coastal town of Cascais near Lisbon - and that their five children attended.

The Instagram entry had more than three million likes within 30 minutes of being posted.

The couple have been together for 10 years, after they met at a Gucci shop in Madrid where Rodríguez was working. He was playing at the Spanish club Real Madrid at the time.

They announced their engagement on 11 August last year, with Rodríguez posting a picture of a huge diamond ring, writing "Yes I do. In this and in all my lives" in her native Spanish.

Ronaldo has five children in total, two of whom he shares with Rodríguez.

She has also helped to raise his other three children, and the family currently live in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh.

The couple's first daughter together, Alana Martina, was born in 2017. Their youngest daughter Bella was born in April 2022, alongside a twin brother, who died .

Ronaldo has scored nearly 1,000 goals in a career which has seen him play for Lisbon-based Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia and Portugal.

Ronaldo, who is currently the captain of the Portuguese football team, recently played in his sixth and final World Cup - a record for appearances in the men's finals which he shares with Lionel Messi of Argentina.

The 41-year-old has won the Ballon d'Or five times, the second-highest number of wins behind Messi who has won the top footballing prize eight times.

His current club Al-Nassr - which he joined in 2022 - confirmed last year that he had signed a new two-year contract , meaning he will stay with the Riyadh-based club until 2027.

Last year, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index valued Ronaldo's net worth at $1.4bn (£1.04bn), making him the first billionaire football player.
