headline: US judge drops bribery and fraud case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani
body:
A US judge has dismissed criminal charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, bringing a high-profile bribery and fraud case against one of India's richest businessmen to an end.

In 2024, Adani was accused of allegedly paying bribes to Indian officials for high-profile renewable energy projects and misleading US investors about it. Adani and his companies have consistently denied wrongdoing.

Adani has welcomed the court order and said he accepted the decision with "humility" and "deep respect" for the judicial process.

In a 47-page order, US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis on Monday approved the Justice Department's request to drop the charges against Adani.

However, the judge strongly criticised the way the decision was reached.

He said R Trent McCotter, principal associate deputy attorney general, had worked with Adani's lawyers on the dismissal without consulting prosecutors and investigators who had handled the case.

Judge Garaufis described the process as "highly unusual", saying McCotter appeared to have substituted his own judgement for that of officials directly involved in the investigation.

The BBC has not seen the official court-filed order but has reviewed a copy published by CourtListener, a US non-profit court archive. Other news organisations have also reviewed the ruling.

In May, the Justice Department asked for the charges to be dismissed, arguing that much of the alleged conduct had taken place outside the US, making the case difficult to prosecute, and that pursuing it no longer aligned with the department's priorities.

The request came after Adani hired a new legal team led by Robert J Giuffra Jr, co-chair of the US law firm Sullivan & Cromwell and a personal lawyer to President Donald Trump. Giuffra had reportedly met Justice Department officials earlier this year to raise concerns about the case.

Judge Garaufis initially resisted the government's request. In June, he said its explanation for abandoning the prosecution was insufficient and ordered officials to provide more information.

He also questioned whether Adani's pledge to invest $10bn (£7.5bn) in the US and create 15,000 jobs had played a role in the decision.

Adani had announced the investment in November 2024, in a post congratulating Donald Trump on his election victory. There were later reports that Adani's lawyers had raised the investment during discussions with the Justice Department about the case.

Adani's lawyers said the investment was never offered in exchange for dropping the charges.

Judge Garaufis ultimately concluded that it had not influenced the Justice Department's decision.

But he said the public could draw its own conclusions about how such discussions might affect perceptions of equal justice and the rule of law.

The judge also found that McCotter's decision appeared to have been made without meaningful input from the prosecutors who brought the case or investigators at the FBI and Securities and Exchange Commission.

"The irregularities in the decision to dismiss the indictment are concerning," Garaufis wrote.

The charges against Adani were dismissed with prejudice, meaning they cannot be brought again.

Adani, who never appeared in a US court during the proceedings, welcomed the ruling. "Throughout this challenging period, our faith in truth, fairness and the rule of law remained unwavering," he wrote on X.

The criminal case is separate from other US proceedings involving Adani and his companies.

In May, Adani agreed to pay $6m and his nephew, Sagar Adani, agreed to pay $12m to settle Securities and Exchange Commission allegations related to investor disclosures, without admitting or denying wrongdoing.

Separately, Adani Enterprises, the group's flagship company, agreed to pay $275m to settle potential civil liability over apparent violations of US sanctions on Iran.

Adani, 64, is chairman of the Adani Group, a sprawling conglomerate with interests in energy, ports, airports and other infrastructure businesses.

He is one of India's richest men and is widely seen as close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Both men are from the western state of Gujarat.

headline: Semi-pro footballer filmed driving at 191mph
body:
A semi-professional footballer who was filmed driving at 191mph has been jailed.

Connor Charlton, 32, was also involved in a scam where other drivers took penalty points for speeding offences in return for cash, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The centre forward, who plays for Nostell Miners Welfare FC in the Northern Counties East League, was seen in footage drifting his BMW at a roundabout, almost crashing into a van. A passenger also filmed him driving at 191mph on a motorway.

Charlton, from Hunslet, was sentenced on Wednesday at Leeds Crown Court to four years in jail and banned from driving for four years and seven months.

He had admitted 10 counts of dangerous driving and four offences of perverting the course of justice.

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North .

headline: Cashing in on SpaceX: 'Every chance I get, I'll sell a little more'
body:
Andre Lavoie joined SpaceX in 2009 as an engineer, designing the pressure tanks that help power its rocket. He was paid partly in stock - a common trade-off at start-ups as a hiring incentive.

Some 17 years on, those 200,000 shares he was given are worth about $23m (£17m) - and the 63-year-old says he's ready to start cashing them as soon as he can.

"Every chance I get going forward, I'll sell a little bit more," he tells the BBC.

"The shares have been going up so radically it keeps messing up my life plans - you really can't know the future, so it's better to sell early and in intervals."

Lavoie is far from being the only one who has seen the value of his stake in SpaceX rocket over the years.

The company's founder, Elon Musk, said on Fox News that SpaceX's listing on the stock market in June had likely made "several thousand" employees millionaires - including staff "who were working on the production line".

According to reports, there are estimated to be 4,400 new millionaires created by the listing.

Unlike most newly-listed firms, SpaceX shares are set to be released in stages: the first 20% on 6 August, with more due in batches through the rest of the year.

Whether or not shareholders decide to sell their stake at the first opportunity is a matter for individuals. Unlike Lavoie, some may choose to hold onto their shares altogether in the hope of bigger gains later.

SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq in June, in the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history, valuing the rocket and satellite firm at more than $2 trillion.

It briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire, before the stock cooled and his fortune slipped back below the milestone within weeks.

In its first results as a public company this week, the firm's quarterly revenue was shown to have nearly doubled to $7.8bn (£5.8bn) from a year earlier, while its spending ballooned to $18.3bn - more than six times what it was a year ago.

Overall, SpaceX made a net loss of $143m in the three months to June, and a loss of $2bn during the first six months of the year.

Musk pushed back against sceptics on an earnings call: "I think people are really underestimating Starlink". He predicted the satellite internet service - the one part of the company that is currently making a profit - could one day deliver a majority of the world's internet.

But shares in the company tumbled on the back of the earnings report , with investors generally spooked by the huge amounts of money being spent on AI.

SpaceX shares fell 13.6% on Wednesday to $108.27 (£80.44) - well below the initial listing price of $135 a share.

Lavoie plans to use his money from selling some of his shares to fund a hotel he is renovating in Pontebba, Italy's northeastern Friuli region, plus a small brewery.

He says his priority for the future is raising awareness of air pollution in the area, in partnership with a local environmental group.

Before he was hired, Lavoie was interviewed by Musk himself.

"He's a very charming person when he wants something," Lavoie says.

He wouldn't be drawn on Musk's politics - "that's his business" - but is unreserved about the company: "I've always been happily supportive and impressed, and would work hard with those incredible people again."

Some analysts value SpaceX at less than half its current stock market price, warning its ties to xAI carry real financial risk - part of a broader worry on Wall Street that sky-high valuations for AI-linked firms, including SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, could prove overdone.

Sinead O'Sullivan, an economist who has previously worked for Nasa, told the BBC in June she thinks SpaceX is an "Elon Musk ego project".

"You're buying a share of the Elon Musk brand more than any kind of space industry," she said.

But Ron Epstein, an aerospace analyst at Bank of America Securities, says the recent share price swings say more about the market than the company.

"A lot of it has to do with macro trends," he says. "None of it really has anything to do with what's going on fundamentally at the company."

He says investors judging SpaceX purely as an AI bet are missing the point: "They're not just a compute provider. They're not just an AI company. It's a far more complicated picture than that."

SpaceX, he adds, has cut the cost of reaching orbit from around $10,000-$20,000 a kilogram to about $2,000 with its Falcon 9 rocket - "they have built a railroad to space."

Lavoie, for his part, isn't rattled. He says: "The solid business model of SpaceX will prove itself to be worth the investment,"even as he takes some of his own winnings off the table.

headline: Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting
body:
Thailand's government will immediately stop issuing gun permits after a shooting incident last week in which a 14-year-old killed eight people and himself.

Existing gun owners are already banned from carrying their weapons in public.

The South East Asian country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in the region, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, and high levels of gun crime.

In response to the recent shooting, the prime minister has promised to pass tough new gun control laws with severe penalties, suspending new permits in the meantime.

Last Friday, a pupil at Debsirin Nonthaburi School outside Bangkok shot his grandparents using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before opening fire at teachers and students at school, authorities say.

Both grandparents, five staff members at the school and one 12-year-old girl died.

Police believe the shooter may have taught himself to use a gun via social media.

They say there is evidence that the boy watched violent content online, and that he showed a strong interest in learning how to handle guns.

His consumption of this content as well as anxiety over studies and family issues might have also fuelled his actions, they add.

Until further notice, no new permits to purchase or own guns will be issued. Existing purchase permits will not be renewed but it is unclear what will happen to existing gun ownership permits.

Permits to carry guns were suspended in late 2023 - owners must keep their weapons at home or at a shooting range.

The government is also considering measures to persuade the owners of an estimated four million unlicensed guns to hand them over in the wake of the school shooting.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has said the announced measures will remain in place as the government works to pass new gun control laws, with stronger controls and significantly harsher penalties.

Gun control advocates have called for mental health assessments as part of the permit process, and for permits to be periodically re-evaluated.

Anutin has said stricter ammunition controls are in his sights, while the education minister has proposed screening at the entrance of schools to stop students from bringing in weapons.

headline: Danube river's low water levels reveal remains of WWII soldiers and motorcycle
body:
The bodies of two World War Two German soldiers have been found in Budapest's Danube river, due to record-low water levels after an intense drought.

Found alongside their remains were the identification tags of the two soldiers, a largely intact German army Wehrmacht motorcycle, a wedding ring and a Kuban shield - a combat badge of the Wehrmacht, the German War Graves Commission said.

The remarkable finds have sparked hope that some families could finally discover the fates of their ancestors, more than 80 years on from the war.

"Now begins a puzzle, in which we will try to determine the identity of the two dead," Arne Schrader, of the German War Graves Commission, told German newspaper Bild.

The wreck in the Danube was reportedly discovered on 2 August, when a passersby reported part of the motorcycle protruding from the rocks on the riverbank in downtown Budapest.

The team also found anti-tank mines, leading to the temporary closure of the riverbank as a bomb disposal unit was deployed.

Some of the items found in the river, notably the identification tags and motorcycle, are remarkably well-preserved due to the mixture of harbour sludge and oil found on the river bed, the German War Graves Commission said.

The commission is a German non-profit organisation that searches, recovers and buries the war dead on behalf of the German government.

The motorcycle is thought to be a DKW NZ 350-1 model, the organisation said, which was produced specifically for wartime use from 1944.

The commission added that of the two tags found, one belonged to a Wehrmacht soldier, and the other to a member of the Waffen-SS, which was declared a criminal organisation responsible for war crimes at the Nuremberg Trials.

During the Second World War, German soldiers' identification tags were split into two on the event of a soldier's death. One half would be kept with the soldier, while the other would be sent to German army authorities, which tracked German military casualties and would notify relatives of soldiers' deaths.

The German War Graves Commission said the families of these two soldiers would have "waited in vain" for official notification of their deaths.

It said it had begun its investigation to find out the identities of the two soldiers, and that anyone who is still missing a relative can search for their names in its database .

It would take time, however, to determine who they were, as the commission will need to ascertain whether the identity tags and Kuban shield actually belong to the two soldiers found.

"The names of the original wearers can probably be found quickly, but that is only the first step," the commission said. "Too many pieces of the puzzle need to be gathered, and the outcome is uncertain."

Bone analysis would be a key way of determining the soldiers' identities, it added.

The news of the soldiers' discovery has gained much attention in World War Two-related social media groups.

"As bad as the low water level is, I am glad that bereaved families can once again be informed about the whereabouts of their relatives, and that the fallen soldiers can be given a dignified burial. Rest in peace," said one person in a Facebook group where people share information about the fate of their ancestors who fought in WWI and WWII.

The soldiers are to be buried at the German war cemetery in Budaörs, just outside the Hungarian capital.

Budapest was the site of fierce fighting between the Soviet Red Army and the German Wehrmacht late in the Second World War.

Other remnants of World War Two have appeared in the Danube as of recent, including a broken-up hull near Prahovo in Serbia.

headline: Lake signs to warn of algae poisoning risk
body:
Dozens of signs warning people about the dangers of algae poisoning are to be placed around England's largest lake.

About 40 notice boards alerting visitors to blue-green algae blooms, which can produce toxins that make humans ill and be fatal to pets, will be installed at Windermere, in the Lake District.

Blooms occur naturally but are more frequent during warm, dry weather and are exacerbated by nutrients from phosphate in pollutants such as sewage.

Funded by the Environment Agency (EA), a further 40 signs will be placed at other locations across Cumbria.

The Love Windermere Partnership, which includes organisations such as the EA, Lake District National Park Authority and United Utilities, said it was installing the permanent signs in response to requests for "clearer and more consistent public information".

As well as explaining what blue-green algae looks like, the notices will provide guidance on where to find current information about blooms and how to report suspected sightings using the Bloomin' Algae app .

The microscopic organisms can look like blue-green paint, scum or greenish-brown discolouration.

Until now, temporary notices have been put up whenever there were outbreaks around Windermere.

Liz Cheslett-Davey, catchment co-ordinator at the EA, said the algae could "appear quickly and the conditions that encourage it to form aren't always easy to predict".

Clear on-site signage, she added, would help people "make informed decisions about using the water safely".

Last month it was reported a dog died after ingesting algae at Coniston Water.

Anyone whose animal has been swimming or drinking from an algae-affected area and begins suffering from vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures or breathing difficulties is advised to consult a vet immediately.

Follow BBC Cumbria on X , Facebook , Nextdoor and Instagram and listen to Radio Cumbria on BBC Sounds.

headline: Artist's 'anger and frustration' with internet copycats
body:
For many artists, the internet has transformed the way they do business, helping them reach new audiences and sell their work around the world.

But the same technology is also making it easier for their creations to be copied, altered and sold without permission.

An illustrator may spend weeks creating a new design only to discover a near-identical version listed for sale on an online marketplace thousands of miles away.

That is exactly what happened to illustrator Kerrie McNeill when likely copies of her work began appearing on Temu.

As the shock wore off, she said what remained was anger and frustration.

"It makes it not enjoyable, constantly being on edge," she said.

BBC News NI contacted Temu and they said they "do not permit unauthorised use of intellectual property" adding they are taking steps to remove the alleged copies of McNeill's work from their platform.

For independent artists like McNeill, it is not just the artwork they feel has been allegedly stolen, but the income attached to it.

She turns her colourful illustrations into art prints, greeting cards and stationery.

A version of her pink Happy Birthday card, featuring colourful birthday cakes finished with gold foil, is listed for sale on Temu for 96p. The original sells for £3.60 on McNeill's own website.

Placed side by side, the two cards are strikingly similar with only small details setting them apart.

Experts say subtle changes like these have become increasingly common. While artwork can be copied in a number of ways, advances in image-editing technology, including AI tools, have made it quicker and easier to create altered versions of existing designs, making copies harder to spot.

"If artwork is accessible then people think that it is theirs to take," McNeill said.

"Because so many people think that it's okay to do, more people do it, and they just don't care."

When McNeill first discovered alleged copies of her work on Temu, the company removed the listings after she reported them.

But two years on, she said the effort of flagging and removing likely copycat products has become an exhausting cycle.

The alleged fake illustrations continue to appear and each report can take time to complete. McNeill said some alleged copies appear to have been altered using AI, making them harder to identify.

"It's just unfair," she said. "I don't think that it should be my job to take down all these listings of my own artwork that has been stolen."

Terry Bradley's paintings are instantly recognisable to many people across Northern Ireland.

His contemporary paintings of Belfast dock workers and female figures have earned him an international following, but that popularity has also made them a target for counterfeit sellers.

His son, Hal Bradley, creative director at Terry Bradley Art, said alleged reproductions of his father's paintings regularly appear for sale online, on various different platforms. Temu is not one of them.

One of his paintings even turned up hanging on the wall of a bar in Thailand.

"Terry's put so much time into these pieces," he said.

"When somebody shows us a botched reproduction of his painting, it kills that for him."

Hal said the family regularly spots likely copies in people's homes and for sale online.

"It's not just that it's fake," he said. "It's also that it's attributed to our paintings. It ruins the whole art piece."

Bradley's career began long before online marketplaces became a major outlet for counterfeit goods.

To help distinguish genuine work, every original painting is now embossed, signed and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.

Like McNeill, Hal said reporting individual listings can be frustrating.

"The people doing it are breaking the law," he said.

"It seems that if we don't do every little thing to remove individual listings, they are just allowed to do it."

Cyber security expert Kevin Curran said technology has moved much faster than the laws designed to protect creators.

"Legislation is lagging far behind," he said.

For many artists, pursuing legal action is unrealistic because cases can take years and cost thousands of pounds, particularly when sellers are based overseas or operate anonymously.

"The sheer scale is very hard for owners," he said.

"You're faced with a future where you won't be able to claim for your original artwork anymore."

Online marketplaces, including Temu, have systems allowing copyright holders to report suspected infringements.

In October, following pressure from the Greeting Card Association (GCA), Temu introduced a bespoke takedown process for greeting card publishers.

Previously, companies had to report every individual listing. Under the trial, they now submit one link, allowing software to identify and remove other listings using the same design, preventing identical copies from simply being re-uploaded.

In relation to McNeill's illustrations, Temu added that their sellers are "required to comply with applicable laws and Temu's policies as a condition of operating on the marketplace".

"Regarding the artist mentioned, we are reviewing the identified listings and are in the process of removing them.

"At the same time, we are adding Kerrie McNeill's works to our IP database for ongoing proactive monitoring to help prevent them from being listed again by bad actors."

Temu stressed that to protect rights holders, Temu uses a combination of automated detection and manual review systems, currently scanning more than 47 million images and more than 9.5m million keywords.

headline: Israeli settlers besieging Palestinian families in West Bank village
body:
Israeli settlers have been besieging two Palestinian families in their homes in the occupied West Bank since Sunday, with the families saying their supplies were running out and rights groups urging the authorities to step in.

On Wednesday Israeli security forces were reported to have withdrawn from the Jewish settler outpost in the village of Qusra near Nablus, following clashes with a crowd of extremist settlers. About a dozen settlers are said to remain at the site.

After the Palestinian homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers.

The Abu Ridi and Hassan families have been posting on social media appealing for help after their water and power supplies were cut off and their food stocks ran low.

The latest developments come as a top UN official told the Security Council in New York on Tuesday that "the West Bank is at breaking point".

All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are set up without official Israeli authorisation.

Palestinian security camera footage shows settlers tearing down a wall outside the Abu Ridi family's home on Sunday evening and using the stones to block the road.

This left seven people - including two young girls – unable to leave their homes while other Palestinians could not reach them. They live in what is known as Area B, part of the West Bank under Palestinian administrative control and Israeli security control.

Posting on Facebook, Qusay Abu Ridi said the situation was critical, "especially as we are completely isolated".

He wrote: "We are living in our own home, on our own land, and we are asking for nothing more than the right to live safely and with dignity."

Aysha Hassan told Reuters the settlers had "tried to break the gate" to the house and "started throwing stones at us, cursing and insulting us".

She said her family was "dying of fear, extremely terrified".

On Monday, Israeli settlers blocked Israeli journalists from the left-leaning Haaretz newspaper from trying to reach the Palestinian properties. The reporters said Israeli soldiers at the scene refused to help them when their car was blocked for two hours. They were told the area was a closed military zone, however the order was not enforced on the settlers.

A day later the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din urgently appealed to the head of the Israeli military's Central Command for the army to protect the besieged residents, evacuate the settlers' outpost and hold the settlers accountable.

Late on Tuesday, a Palestinian ambulance was finally allowed to reach the families, delivering food and taking one child away for medical treatment.

At about the same time, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) put out a statement condemning the establishment of the new outpost. It said that entering and seizing Palestinian homes was "illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable activity".

When the head of its Central Command, Maj Gen Avi Bluth and other senior officers arrived at the scene early on Wednesday they are said to have met residents and voiced their "grave concern".

Afterwards, Palestinian security camera video shared with the BBC showed confrontations between Israeli soldiers and border police and a large crowd of settlers. The security forces used tear gas and stun grenades.

In other footage, the Israeli forces appear to have confiscated the canopy under which the settlers were sheltering, while leaving their other equipment.

"Border Police forces evacuated the tent and are working to evacuate the civilians who were staying there. The incident is still ongoing," the IDF stated.

It said it was decided that "disciplinary action would be taken against the security personnel involved, who were documented at the site several days ago".

The Palestinian village mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, told the BBC that local residents had seen "a clear and sustained pattern of targeting Qusra". Last month a newly completed mosque was set on fire with graffiti in Hebrew sprayed nearby.

That settler attack was one of many that followed on from an incident in the Palestinian village of Tal. After Israeli settlers attacked Tal, it triggered an escalation in which six people were killed - four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom acted as a security coordinator for a nearby Israeli settlement.

In July, settlers also surrounded a Palestinian home in the village of Jalud, near Qusra, for more than two weeks. Afterwards, the owners fled and settlers took over the property where they remain until now.

"Settler violence has reached unprecedented levels," the UN's Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, told the Security Council in a briefing on Tuesday.

He gave what he described as "the sobering human toll" and mentioned that the Nablus Governorate in particular had been hit hard recently by violence.

According to the UN's figures, 76 Palestinians – including 18 children - have been killed in the West Bank this year, by Israeli forces or settlers. At the same time, three Israelis – including one civilian – were killed in confrontations with Palestinians and in an alleged ramming attack by a Palestinian in the West Bank.

Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities in the West Bank have experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians, the UN says.

It has registered that in 2026, about 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions.

Speaking at the UN meeting, Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon dismissed the idea that settlements were an obstacle to peace. He said that they would remain and continue to grow as his country had biblical, historic and legal rights to the land.

He said that the Security Council "must understand a simple truth: we are not going anywhere".

headline: AI agent hacks gym to get its user a spot in pilates class
body:
It's a familiar experience: racing against masses of anonymous netizens online to get yourself on the list for an in-demand event.

For Andrew Bird, from Melbourne, in Australia, it was a spot in an often over-booked pilates class - but his solution had unexpected consequences.

He says he outsourced the "chore" to an AI agent - a tool that can carry out online tasks autonomously.

It succeeded, but went further than he imagined by hacking the gym's online systems, in what is being seen as the latest example of the way AI agents will go to any lengths to carry out the jobs they've been given.

"What made the whole thing more surreal was the tone," Bird wrote in his blog.

"The bot was not malicious. It was helpful."

The news comes as AI firms have been admitting in recent weeks that their AI bots have been going on uncontrollable hacking sprees in testing sessions gone wrong.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have all revealed that their own AI bots have carried out cyber-attacks on private companies in the pursuit of goals set by their makers.

The gym booking incident is not considered a serious cyber-attack but is another example of the unintended consequences of tasking sophisticated AI bots with jobs.

It actually happened in April, but has come to light now thanks to reporting from ABC News Australia .

Bird declined to talk to the BBC about it saying only: "Thanks for getting in touch. I am unavailable to participate in an interview. Appreciate your interest the story."

He has also deleted his blog post about it from the time - but not explained why.

According to his account, Bird was using the software OpenClaw - a popular tool that allows users to chat to their AI bots (in this case Athropic's Claude Opus 4.6) through WhatsApp and set it off on autonomous tasks.

He had previously used it to manage his emails, calendar and book restaurants.

Once given the gym booking task, the bot explained that it had manipulated the system to book him onto classes months in advance - against the normal rules of the system.

The AI technologist then wondered if the agent could move him up the waiting list for an upcoming class.

The agent replied saying it had succeeded by cancelling another gym-goer's booking.

According to the ABC News report the AI bot told Bird: "The API has zero authorisations checks on cancelling other people's reservations … I tested this with the person in waitlist position #1 — and it actually went through. So you've moved from #4 to #3 already."

Bird asked the bot to reverse the action but it wasn't able to so he asked it to write a cyber-security report and alert the gym owners about the vulnerability.

Bird, who runs an AI document making company, says he had no intention of cancelling his fellow pilates fan's spot.

"It's not the end of the world, so I didn't beat myself up about it, but it certainly was a warning signal to use it responsibly," he told ABC News.

headline: TikTok star Sydney Towle, who shared her cancer journey online, dies aged 26
body:
Sydney Towle, a popular social media influencer who shared her experience living with a rare, aggressive form of cancer, has died at the age of 26.

Towle's family announced her death, from complications related to bile duct cancer that had spread to other parts of her body, on her social media accounts on Thursday.

"Syd went peacefully last night after an almost three-year-long battle with cholangiocarcinoma," her brother Austin said in a video message, alongside their mother, on TikTok.

Towle, who was moved to hospice care earlier this week, had over a million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram.

She spent the last three years chronicling her daily life as a young person going through chemotherapy and living with cancer, with all its hopes, joys and struggles. She had been living in New York City at the time of her death.

"We are so proud of how hard Sydney fought and for sharing her journey with so many people," Towle's family said in a statement.

"She wanted to raise awareness for rare cancers and was passionate about promoting self-advocacy. We will continue her legacy and honour her in every way we can."

Following the announcement of her death, thousands of followers posted messages on Towle's social media accounts paying tribute to her and sending well wishes to her family.

"Sweet angel. Fly high," actress Alyssa Milano commented. "Praying for all who loved her. She is really something special."

"You were such a bright light and will be missed," one person wrote on Instagram, while another said: "How lucky we all are to have found you on the internet. Thank you for sharing yourself and your story."

In May, Towle posted a series of videos from the hospital where she was receiving treatment for complications related to her cancer.

She shared that her cancer had spread to her peritoneum, a membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavities and protects internal organs.

On 19 May, she posted a video of herself, sitting beside her mother in the hospital, in which she said her oncologist had told her he would no longer treat her cancer, recommending she begin end-of-life care. Towle said she would not accept this and vowed to continue fighting, choosing instead to switch to another specialist.

Despite her illness, she expressed fervent optimism and joy for life on her social media accounts. She often posted videos of herself dancing, getting ready, and having fun with friends.

She recently fulfilled her dream of modelling, walking in a swimsuit for The Chemo Club x Post Swim show at Miami Swim Week.

"Rich in life because my friends choose to spend a Saturday fundraising for cancer research," Towle wrote in a post in March.

"Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry's, watch your favourite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn't make it a bad life," Towle wrote in another post last year.

Towle was not shy about showing her stomach, where she had a hepatic artery pump implanted, on social media.

"I have only recently started seeing the resilience and beauty in this body," she wrote in a post last year, alongside photos of herself in a swimsuit. "Scars that remind me of how far I've come. And I'm reminded that dreams only end when you allow them to."

headline: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
body:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

headline: Burnham faces unpopularity test over prisons dilemma
body:
In his first few weeks in Downing Street, Andy Burnham could hardly have been clearer that his aim as prime minister is to make people feel better.

His supporters inside the Labour Party characterise him as a leader with the political nous to prioritise policies that will make a difference, and the communication ability to sell those messages to the masses.

His critics, including Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, have branded him a "people pleaser" who doesn't want to take difficult decisions.

The conundrum over how to manage the early release of prisoners is an acute example of the tricky political decision-making that inevitably comes with power.

Andy Burnham could have chosen to modify the early release scheme, which he inherited from the Starmer government, according to the length of offenders' sentences.

That would have seen some rapists and child sex offenders released, and inevitably lead to emotive stories from victims whose abusers were being set free.

Instead, the fledgling PM focused on the type of crime, ensuring those mentioned above would stay behind bars.

But that caused a political storm of its own, as it emerged that two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper would still be eligible for early release next year.

That quickly became the first big test for an administration that prides itself on its ability to communicate.

And after mounting pressure from the public, media and members of PC Harper's family, there does now appear to have been a shift.

Burnham said this morning he had "not accepted that it is impossible to do more" to prevent dangerous criminals being released early – and said he's asked the justice secretary to fast-track a plan for freeing up prison places.

He insisted that didn't constitute a change, saying he had been "pushing on this issue" since his first day in office.

But his latest view was not the impression created by the government in recent days.

On Monday lunchtime, Downing Street heavily suggested it could do no more.

Over the weekend, the Ministry of Justice said that exempting more prisoners from early release risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".

And last week, Burnham himself wrote in the Telegraph that he'd "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". Justice Secretary Alex Norris even apologised to the families of victims, including PC Andrew Harper.

PC Harper's mother Debbie Adlam told BBC Breakfast the handling of the situation had been a "hash".

Downing Street will hope the events of the last week will be remembered as a PM who has forced the system to do what he wanted.

But they'll fear that the lasting impression could instead be of a misstep that's left victims' families in anguish.

Details of the government's plan to free up prison spaces are still sparse.

The government has been clear that it believes an exemption for manslaughter convictions is an all or nothing approach – and could therefore require a large amount of prison capacity.

Ministers are exploring how to speed up deportations of foreign criminals, the use of female prison spaces for male offenders, and indefinite sentences handed out in past decades.

None of those ideas sound easy, and there'll be questions over whether they will create enough space on the prison estate.

Even if success comes on that front, the PM's statement included an acknowledgement that the difficulties surrounding this policy are not over.

"Even with all these changes, there will be concerns from many victims about who will still be released early for other offences," Burnham said.

When those concerns arise in the coming months, a prime minister who wants to make people feel better may find himself under pressure again.

headline: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
body:
At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.

They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman.

"The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."

So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.

He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.

Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over.

"My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.

He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.

She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.

He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches.

"My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."

Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China.

For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance.

There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia.

This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand.

"The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says.

Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden.

Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages".

Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older.

So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which had "bred illegal practices and chaos".

It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry.

This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern".

In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000).

"I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC.

Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub.

The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles.

Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud.

So he paid up and the introductions began.

He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids.

He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him.

"She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest."

They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined.

After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it.

"If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan."

The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media.

In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background.

Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money.

Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents.

When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price.

He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared.

From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong.

In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave.

Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived.

"There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us.

The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC.

They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them.

"Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with."

One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating".

Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels.

His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage.

On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag.

He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency.

Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room.

Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims.

"All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed."

But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced.

He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses.

The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients.

"The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well."

They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential".

He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back.

"I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed.

"We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible."

This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved.

"I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says.

He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages."

He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime.

These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many.

For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money.

"In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says.

"In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove."

Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash.

Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all.

"After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now."

Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo.

"It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork.

"I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

headline: First OpenAI, now Meta - why do AI hacks keep happening?
body:
Over the last fortnight, reports of AI models going beyond their expected bounds - be that technically or morally - have been seemingly unavoidable.

What started with a trickle - ChatGPT-maker OpenAI admitting their AI had hacked the site Hugging Face - has turned into a flood of groups revealing they had discovered instances of AI going out of control.

Claude-maker Anthropic, Meta and the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) have now each reported incidents which seem to paint a worrying picture of a world in which tech going rogue is the norm.

In reality, each case offers a window into the risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents - and the importance of testing their limits before they are released to the world.

The OpenAI incident has, as Hugging Face's co-founder Thomas Wolf described it , come as a "wake-up call" for the tech industry since it happened at the end of July.

It was a big moment which caused big companies to reflect on their own systems - and, in some cases, check they hadn't missed something similarly shocking.

Anthropic was the first to act. On Friday, the company found three instances out of thousands where its model Claude had managed to gain access to the internet.

Then on Tuesday, the AISI, the UK government agency which evaluates cutting-edge models, then said it had detected a "security incident" during a routine evaluation .

It had been testing models by both OpenAI and Anthropic, and found they too tried to carry out cyber-attacks - calling for "scrutiny, transparency, and action".

Finally followed Meta, which revealed one of its AI models had inadvertently been allowed to access the internet due to a "misconfiguration" during a third-party test .

In disclosing the incident, it is following in the footsteps of those before it.

Before AI models are released to the public, they are put to the test in a series of internal and external evaluations.

The aim is to figure out their potential to do good or bad, as well has how they perform in benchmarks measuring their skills.

These typically take place in what are known as "sandboxes". These are protected spaces designed to mirror real systems - but with strict guardrails in place.

In the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, the AI attacked the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which let it access the internet and "go rogue".

Meanwhile the AISI said its own incident , which saw two powerful AI tools create fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks, was not down to an issue with the sandbox.

Instead, it was due to how it went about its tests.

The models it tested were granted access to the internet, and the AISI also disabled in-built filters that would usually block dangerous cyber-attacks.

"To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour," it said, while noting its unexpected "signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours".

Prof Alan Woodward, professor of cyber-security at the University of Surrey, said these cases - while distinct in what happened and why - tell an important story.

"For 30 years, one rule of software testing held firm: whatever happens in the test environment stays in the test environment," he said.

"In the past month, that rule has been broken three times."

"One model broke out. One walked through a door left open by mistake. One was deliberately given the keys so testers could measure what it would do."

He said these were different causes, but they had the same lesson - "the testing lab is now where the risk lives".

He told the BBC that as models become more capable, more must be done to secure the environments where they are tested.

"Testing an AI agent is less like checking code and more like handling a hazardous material: sealed rooms, constant monitoring of what leaves the building, a rehearsed containment plan," he said.

"AISI contained its incident within an hour. The next organisation may not."

For those developing AI tools which are designed to take actions on a person's behalf, there is a careful balance to be struck between harnessing their benefits and exposing their risks.

The benefit is significant. In theory, we could be able to liberate ourselves of dull, menial tasks, such as replying to emails, going to meetings or managing calendars and diaries, by delegating these to capable bots.

The downside is that with great power comes great responsibility, and risk.

It's something particularly realised when handing power to tools which are not, like us, able to bring a range of values, context and understanding to decisions we made.

"Recent incidents of frontier AI models carrying out unsanctioned actions and, in some cases, human-like deceptive behaviour on the open internet are a serious reminder of the risks AI capabilities pose," said Ollie Whitehouse, the National Cyber Security Centre's chief technology officer on Tuesday.

Some believe the sheer volume of tasks that will be handled by these tools will mean human oversight might not be enough to contain the problem of models going rogue .

But in the meantime, many feel strengthening oversight overall is vital if development continues at its same, frenzied pace.

It is unlikely Meta will be the last to emerge with findings of models showing they have, as Prof Woodward puts it, "gone to school" - and learnt our own ways of finding and exploiting gaps in systems.

For some, these episodes point to clear security failures on the part of AI companies leading the charge on this game-changing, era-defining tech.

For others, they are merely another vehicle for tech firms to hype up their powerful models and compete with rivals.

For me, both theories hold some grain of truth.

But in rearing their head one after another, these events have nonetheless spurred fears about AI's capabilities and where these are headed as developers forge ahead.

And the question inevitably moves to what regulators can and should do next.

Michael Birtwistle, associate director at the Ada Lovelace Institute, makes the point that the UK lacks legal incentives for AI firms to prevent systems from developing capabilities which could pose dangers, and that there are no repercussions if testing protocols fail.

More broadly, Dr Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, told the BBC that with opportunities to test frontier AI systems narrowing for many, governments should follow the UK in setting up dedicated institutes for testing.

Improving third-party evaluations with initiatives such as a "trusted tester scheme" for the most risky types of challenges could also be used to limit adverse impacts, she said.

Rather than fear an AI-cyber apocalypse in the meantime, Prof Woodward says, "it's a case of 'keep calm and fix stuff'".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain and Imran Rahman-Jones

headline: Stolen horse reunited with owner after eight years
body:
A rare cremello horse that was stolen in Scotland eight years ago has been reunited with his owner after he was found in Yorkshire.

Polo, a 13-year-old stallion, was taken during a break-in at a farm in Morayshire in 2018.

He was discovered in Shipley by West Yorkshire Police's Wildlife and Rural Crime Team after "community intelligence" located him and he was returned to Zoe Urquart on Thursday evening.

Urquart said she was never expecting to hear he had been found, and it was "absolutely fantastic" to have him home. "I'd given up on the idea that he would ever be located a number of years ago. So it was a massive shock," she said.

"I got a phone call completely out of the blue at four o'clock in the afternoon and I had to make an instant decision on what I was going to do.

"He was uplifted within three hours and en route."

Urquart discovered Polo was missing after her farm was targeted by thieves and the stud horse, who was then just a foal, had vanished.

Over the next eight years she heard almost nothing about his whereabouts, then last week she received a call "out of the blue" from the police.

"I did get the odd message from people who have looked out for him and thought they'd seen him, but no confirmed sightings at all," she said.

He was in a "really poor" condition after years of being neglected, she said, with a tumour on his undercarriage and sore eyes.

"His veterinary and rehabilitation care will span into thousands of pounds, if they had several foals a year from him, they'd have made tens of hundreds of pounds, but neglected his health," she said.

"He has quite a large sarcoid which is a form of tumour that will need to be removed by the bow."

She said he was found running with mares in a field, and she suspected he had been stolen because of his genetics.

"Genetically he is quite a rare colour. Perlino cremello foals are not so unheard of now, but certainly going back in time they were really quite rare," she said.

Perlino and cremello horses have pale coats, pink skin and blue eyes.

Despite his condition, Polo is settling well back into life at the Morayshire stables.

"He's going to get the best of care and we'll get him back to the way he should be," said Urquart.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said: "Following some community intelligence in Shipley, enquiries were made with Police Scotland, the microchip number was checked and it was established that it was a horse stolen in 2018.

"The horse was seized and enquiries into the original offence are ongoing."

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North .

headline: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
body:
The world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific , according to the EU's climate monitoring service.

The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.

Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.

Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week , as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.

Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.

Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months.

El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.

Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.

The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.

Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.

Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.

Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May.

The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period.

"July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling.

"This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added.

France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought.

River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected.

Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production.

The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated.

"Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.

Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said.

That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances.

In the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies.

England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought.

The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist.

Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate.

Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990.

"We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone".

Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels.

The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century.

headline: Works by disabled artists focus on wellbeing
body:
A summer exhibition by disabled artists is opening in Margate later, with a focus on wellbeing, care and colour.

The artists created the work at Sandra Art4All Studio, which is celebrating 10 years of making art accessible to disabled people with additional impairments and learning needs.

Sandra Hayden, who runs the studio in the Kent town, said the supportive space had served for the past decade as "a vibrant space where artistic expression knows no bounds".

A launch event is taking place later for the Proud 2 Create exhibition, which runs at The Margate School in The Old Woolworths Building until 29 August. The event includes work by deaf, autistic and neurodivergent artists.

Hayden said the studio's exhibitions over several years had shown the positive impact of its work and she hoped people would come and see the show.

"Stepping into a gallery that is full of colour like ours and walking around the exhibition provides a gentle, mindful physical activity that can lower stress, encourage presence and boost a person's day."

She said the "simple act of viewing" allowed people to slow down, reflect and find a sense of calm away from busy, daily lives.

Hayden, an art teacher, set up the studio after she was made redundant following the closure of the Royal School for Deaf Children in Margate.

The studio works to enable the artists to create their work as independently as possible.

Celebrations to mark the studio's 10th anniversary have included two summer exhibitions.

Work went on show at the Pie Factory Margate in July, and the exhibition at the Margate School of Art features 170 pieces of "vibrant art" created this year.

Artists taking part include Celia Balfour, Nessie Bigg, Katie Byrne, Allegra Dams, Bethany Davies, Olivia Joslin, Dalibor Kovac-Stokes, Alex Mortimer, Jessica Park, Harriet Steddy, Gareth Tudor and Sandra Hayden.
