headline: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
body:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”

Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.

She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.

Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.

Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview the stars.

"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”

Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers such as Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal, Tom Hiddleston and Zendaya herself – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.

She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.

It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).

She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.

Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.

"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.

For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.

She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.

"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"

"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."

But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.

"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".

She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.

Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".

With 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough.

"There's always hate in this industry," she says.

But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones.

"If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."

For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters.

"The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says.

"And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says.

"I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

headline: Burnham considers disposable BBQ ban over wildfire risks
body:
Andy Burnham has said the government is considering a ban on disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

Some retailers have already decided to voluntarily stop selling the devices, which have previously attracted warnings from fire chiefs.

It comes as Burnham chairs an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures in recent months.

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

Speaking during a visit to Stevenage, Burnham said a disposable barbecue ban was something the government was "certainly going to consider".

"I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires," he added.

Burnham did not specify whether the government was considering a restriction on the sale of disposable BBQs, or limitations on their use.

A Labour MP wrote to large retailers last week in a bid to stop them selling disposable barbecues for the rest of the summer, whilst a number of Lib Dem MPs have also backed restrictions.

The National Farmers Union has also called on local councils to issue public space protection orders to restrict their use in public areas.

Authorities including Brighton & Hove and Fylde, in Lancashire, are among councils to have used these orders to ban single-use grills in recent years.

Those who defy such orders can currently be fined up to £100, a limit that is set to rise to £500 in future.

Councils intending to issue the orders are required to consult residents beforehand, and gather evidence of an ongoing risk to quality of life in a particular area.

The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.

There has already been one Cobra meeting on heatwaves this year chaired by officials, but this will be the first such emergency session chaired by Burnham.

In June, the government under previous prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced that specialist firefighters would be positioned in key locations across England in response to wildfire risks, with forces encouraged to use a government fund to upgrade equipment.

Burnham had faced calls from the Green Party to chair a Cobra meeting on the heatwaves, with leader Zack Polanksi accusing the prime minister of inaction amid threats to public health and food supplies.

Speaking on Wednesday, Polanski welcomed the meeting but said it was "not enough just to discuss" the threats from heat.

He added that recent temperatures showed the need to offer workers flexible hours to allow them to avoid the hottest part of the day, and for a legally-enforced maximum temperature for workplaces.

The party has previously called for more publicly accessible "cool spaces" for vulnerable groups and financial support to help households heatproof their homes.

Fire chiefs have said that wildfires are becoming a "recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities" amid a changing climate.

Crews responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record.

headline: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear to work?
body:
Yet another summer heatwave could be on the way to make your commute sweaty and your workplace stuffy.

What to wear to work in the summer can be a surprisingly difficult decision. Shorts, strappy tops and sandals may keep you cool - but will they be judged too casual, revealing or unprofessional?

There's a bare-legged backlash in Tokyo where officials encouraged men to swap suits for shorts at work , prompting complaints about hairy legs in the office.

So what is acceptable to wear to work, how can you successfully style your summer wardrobe and can your boss tell you what you can and can't wear?

Conor, who works in media, has regularly worn shorts to the office during the recent hot weather. "Who gives a monkey's what you wear?" he says.

"If you're able to do your job safely, professionally and appropriately, there's a lot to be said for letting people be comfortable."

And many seem to agree - a recent poll by market research firm Ipsos found 62% of adults thought it was acceptable for men to wear shorts to work in hot weather, while 63% said the same for women.

But we aren't talking short-shorts or denim hot pants fashion designer Amanda Wakeley points out: "If you're asking yourself whether they're too short, they probably are".

She says shorts are "the trickiest item to get right in a professional environment" and recommends tailored, longer shorts paired with a crisp shirt or lightweight blazer for both men and women.

Stylist Clare Chambers agrees shorts should sit around the kneecap for both men and women. For men, she recommends tailored chino-style shorts with an untucked T-shirt or shirt.

Wakeley describes flip-flops as one of the few definite "no" items in most offices. "They instantly signal leisure rather than professionalism and can make even the most polished outfit feel underdressed," she says.

Chambers agrees, and says even during the hottest weather, woven flats are a better option because they are breathable while still covering the foot.

Almost two-thirds of people questioned by Ipsos said they were unacceptable for men in the workplace, while 58% said the same for women.

Sandals, however, are a slightly different matter as Wakeley says refined leather sandals can be entirely acceptable in many offices, provided they are clean and well maintained.

The difference, she says, is whether they look like part of a considered outfit or something that would normally be worn around a swimming pool.

She adds that while socks and sandals have become a viral fashion trend "it's important to consider whether a trend aligns with the image you want to communicate professionally".

"This combination can read as highly casual and youthful, which may unintentionally detract from giving you a credible and authoritative presence."

Some 40% of adults considered tank tops or vest tops acceptable for women at work, compared with only 24% who said the same for men, according to Ipsos.

Natasia, a teacher in London, says at a previous school she and other staff had been summoned "regularly in the summer months to tell us off about our outfits."

She says she was also told to cover up her tattoos. "It should be OK to have your arms out at work especially when it's hot," she says.

Wakeley says a well-cut camisole or strappy top can work when worn beneath a linen overshirt, lightweight jacket or tailored co-ord. On its own, however, it may feel too informal.

Chambers says if you're wearing a strappy top "you must wear a strapless bra as it utterly kills an outfit when you can see bra straps".

She explains that thicker straps are a safer option where the dress code is unclear and recommends satin camisoles as a more polished alternative to basic cotton vests.

She adds that while bandeau tops are "such an on-trend look this summer, they are a no-go for work".

"The constant need to keep fiddling to pull them up displays an uncomfortable and unconfident demeanour," she says.

Wakeley and Chambers both say that you don't need to lose your personal style when dressing for the office and you can still inject plenty of personality while following a dress code. Here are their top tips on how to style summer clothes for the office.

Climate change is expected to bring more severe, frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves in UK summers in the coming years.

Employers are allowed to set standards around clothing and appearance, particularly where there are legitimate reasons such as safety, branding or maintaining a professional image.

But employment lawyer Sarah Tahamtani says dress codes should be "reasonable, proportionate and capable of justification".

"During extreme heat, employers should consider whether existing requirements remain practical and whether greater flexibility can be introduced."

They must also consider employees with disabilities, medical conditions or other vulnerabilities that may be worsened by high temperatures.

An employee who believes a request is unreasonable or inconsistently applied should first raise the issue with a manager or HR and explain how the rule is affecting their comfort or ability to work safely.

headline: I was accused of using AI in my dissertation but I wrote it all myself
body:
In August last year, medical student Harrison Sharples was "shocked" to receive an academic misconduct alert saying the dissertation he had spent his summer writing had been flagged as being AI-generated.

The 20-year-old University of St Andrews student could not understand how the markers had thought the work wasn't his own.

He told the BBC he hadn't even considered using AI as he had plenty of time to complete the assignment and had enjoyed writing it.

"I tend to honestly just forget that it's an option for me to use," he said.

According to the university his dissertation on the impact of play therapy on reducing anxiety in hospitalised children was assessed by two human markers.

One of them raised concerns over the potential use of AI.

The marker's notes - seen by the BBC - raise concerns about the "polished/uniform tone" of the work, noting the "consistent flawless grammar and similar sentence structure with no variation in style".

The notes also mention a "formulaic paragraph structure that follows a typical AI pattern of 'general claim, the example/result, and conclusion'."

Other observations point to repetitive phrasing and a lack of "nuanced critique" as well as a high usage of "em" dashes, a type of punctuation thought to be favoured by AI models.

As a result of the marker's concerns, Harrison was given a date to attend a virtual hearing with a panel from the university's school of medicine to defend his case.

He says he prepared well to provide the evidence and defend his case but, on the day, the link to the virtual hearing did not arrive on time.

After emailing the university, he received the link five minutes after the start time for the hearing.

"At this point, I'm extremely nervous about it because I'm thinking this is my one chance to prove myself, to redeem myself - and they're going to think that I'm just not showing up," he said.

During the half-hour hearing the student was asked to define the medical terms he used in his dissertation, which Harrison says was a surprise.

"I was so shook up about my start to the hearing," he said.

"I don't think I represented myself completely well."

A week later, he received the decision that the allegations of AI usage had been upheld.

This meant his mark would be capped at seven, just enough to pass, and the matter may have to be declared when applying to the GMC for provisional registration.

"That was the thing which pushed me to appeal," Harrison said.

The university accepted the appeal, recognising that the late arrival of the link affected his ability to present his case. He was invited to attend another hearing in mid-November.

Harrison says that it was held in a similar way to the first one, except this time the panel's questions were on his approach to writing.

"It went a lot smoother," he said.

"I think I was a lot more clear in putting across my points."

This time the university decided not to uphold the allegations.

"I felt so relieved," Harrison said.

"It would just be really stressful to constantly have that strike on my record."

He eventually got his full mark for his dissertation and the case will not impact his professional record. But Harrison says he was consumed by worries throughout the whole of that semester and it affected his studies.

He says he had a support network of friends, girlfriend and family from back home in Manchester but the situation impacted him on "an inside level".

"There was so much time when I just didn't know what was happening and I think that is what caused me the most worry and stress about it," he said.

"It was so big in my mind it didn't allow me to think about anything else. That's why I neglected my studies because I just got pushed out of operating space in my brain."

Harrison had to defer his exams for a semester and sit them in the middle of the summer. As a result, his graduation has been delayed until December.

"I would be graduating if it wasn't for what happened to me," he said.

AI ethics advisor Sidrah Hassan told the BBC that AI large language models (LLMs) are progressing "at light speed" and it is difficult for institutions to keep up.

"There are tell-tale signs that AI systems tend to use in their outputs that can help you figure out if this is AI-generated or human-generated," she said.

But existing AI detection tools are not robust and have a high error rate, she said.

Human markers can flag them if they are unsure but Hassan says that catching students out may not be the future-proof solution.

"I think that's not the point," she said. "We should be changing the way we test them because as humans we'll always try to find the easy way to do something."

A statement from the University of St Andrews said : "We would not comment on the details of individual cases, but can confirm that, in this instance, the decision to uphold the student's appeal related solely to a procedural issue concerning the arrangements for the hearing.

"We are working both within the university and across the sector to support the responsible use of AI in academic work, including in medicine."

headline: Bondi Beach shooting hero's assault charges dropped by police
body:
A man who was hailed a hero for disarming one of the Bondi Beach shooters in December has had assault charges against him dropped by police.

Ahmed al Ahmed was charged in June with domestic violence common assault, as well as stalking and intimidation, after an alleged incident with his father in March at a home in southwest Sydney. Ahmed denied both charges.

On Wednesday, in a local Sydney court, prosecutors withdrew the charges after it was agreed that Ahmed would abide by an apprehended domestic violence order for 12 months, limiting his contact with his father.

Outside the court, Ahmed, 44, welcomed the development, telling reporters that he was a "free man" and that he hoped for "peace".

Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr said in court that the order prohibiting Ahmed from assaulting, threatening, stalking or intimidating his father had been accepted without admissions, according to national broadcaster ABC.

Ahmed made global headlines last year after footage emerged of him tackling one of two gunmen who had opened fire during a Jewish event at Sydney's Bondi Beach, killing 15 people.

Ahmed wrestled a firearm from Sajid Akram and was later shot several times by a second alleged gunman, Naveed Akram.

The attack marked Australia's deadliest mass shooting in decades, and police later declared it a terrorist incident targeting the Jewish community.

A fundraiser in the days after the shooting raised more than AU$2.5m ($1.7m; £1.24m) for Ahmed, who also received a bedside visit from Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

In a separate court matter, two of Ahmed's brothers were recently charged over allegations they threatened him and tried to extort some of the donations he had received.

headline: The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer
body:
Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of The Office, has revealed she has "incurable" breast cancer.

Davis, the daughter of comedian Jasper Carrott, appeared frequently as the sympathetic and witty office receptionist in the groundbreaking mockumentary, from 2001 to 2003.

A post from the 53-year-old actress on Instagram on Tuesday said: "I wanted to share something with you all that I've kept to myself for a while but for various reasons would like to share now.

"A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, which has metastasized [spread] to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo."

She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."

The actress noted how she "almost didn't bother getting it checked", urging followers not to "ignore anything" and to "get everything checked out".

She continued: "As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there's a lot I have learned from it, and I'm grateful for that.

"I'm not scared of whatever comes next. I'm at peace with it. I'll see my [late dog] Gracie sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it's far harder for them than for me."

Davis added: "I still would like to keep working. I'm perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life."

Following her post to Instagram, Davis received an outpouring of support from fans and well-wishers.

The Office US star Jenna Fischer wrote: "Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let's spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort!"

Fischer played receptionist Pam Beesly on the subsequent American version of the show, with Davis having playing the character's UK counterpart.

In 2024, Fischer revealed she had been diagnosed with breast cancer a year earlier, but that she was cancer-free after undergoing chemotherapy, radiation therapy and a lumpectomy.

Olympic cycling champion Sir Chris Hoy, who is living with a terminal prostate cancer diagnosis , offered: "Keep going Lucy!"

Birmingham-born Davis played Dawn, who was also the love interest of Tim Canterbury, played by Martin Freeman in Ricky Gervais's classic TV sitcom - which last month celebrated its 25th anniversary.

Gervais replied to her Instagram post by dropping a love heart emoji in the comments section.

After The Office, Davis went on to feature as Dianne in 2004 comedy-horror film Shaun of the Dead and Etta Candy in 2017's Wonder Woman, as well as Hilda Spellman in Netflix series The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina.

More recently, she played Eva in the Disney Channel's action-comedy series The Villains of Valley View.

In her Instagram post - which was accompanied by a video of her reading a poem while ringing a bell in hospital - she went on to say she intended to keep up her work supporting animal rights, which is "so important to me".

She went on: "I still would like to keep working. I'm perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life.

"For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose."

According to Cancer Research UK , stage four breast cancer is a cancer that starts in the breast tissue but spreads to another part of the body, making it incurable. Treatment can control the cancer for some years, however.

The main symptoms of breast cancer in women may include a lump, or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit, the NHS website says .

Symptoms can also include a change in the skin of your breast such as dimpling or redness, a change in size or shape of one or both breasts, and/or nipple discharge, which may have blood in it.

Other symptoms may include a change in the shape or look of the nipple, such as it turning inwards or a rash on it.

headline: Park renaming to honour club's old stadium
body:
Land on the site of Coventry City's former Highfield Road stadium is set to be renamed Highfield Road Park, in tribute to the club's historic home.

The Sky Blues played their final match at the stadium in 2005 after 106 years at the ground, with the stadium demolished the following year and redeveloped for housing.

Pete Witherow, of the Sky Blue Archive, said campaigners have spent the past two years working with the city council to secure the tribute in the centre of Signet Square.

A consultation was carried out with local residents and fans, he added.

The renaming forms part of a wider effort to preserve the memory of Highfield Road.

Plans are also in place for Coventry's first dementia bench, which organisers hope will be installed next year, Witherow said.

The bench will feature a plaque and QR code linking visitors to the Coventry Dementia Hub and encourage people to reminisce and share memories.

In addition, four vision boards are planned for the site, displaying photographs showing the former stadium alongside images of the housing development that replaced it.

The organiser said the inspiration came partly from Arsenal's redevelopment of its former Highbury stadium site.

"That was the blueprint I took to the council," Witherow said.

"I think Highfield Road Park should be a tourist attraction for fans who used to go to the ground."

The group has already overseen the restoration of a commemorative plaque and plinth at the site after it was vandalised.

Witherow, a lifelong Coventry City supporter and season ticket holder, said the project was personal.

"I've got some great memories there," he said.

"The first game I really remember was travelling up on my own when I was very young.

"I hadn't told my parents, I just said I was going to the local shop and they were pulling their hair out when I got back, but I was that passionate about going.

"I can't remember how old I was but it was two pence on the bus".

Witherow said several organisations and individuals have helped bring the project to fruition, including LFE Engineering, who built the new park sign.

The sign was handed over to the council, which will arrange for its installation.

"We're not sure of the exact date yet because it's down to the council when they can carry out the work," he said.

headline: In Pictures: Wing-walking, waterspouts and the Proms
body:
A daredevil 97-year-old has been spotted high in the sky in Gloucestershire, strapped to a plane in a Guinness World Record-breaking attempt.

As the summer holidays go by in a warm haze, a bit of magic has been created across Bristol's city centre with several handmade fairy doors hidden in plain sight.

And we have experienced some incredible weather phenomenons across the region, including a rare waterspout and cloud iridescence.

Here are some of the West's highlights in pictures.

Big performances: Hundreds of ticket holders have been enjoying music at the Bristol Beacon and St George's as the BBC Proms returned to the city once again. The proms continue into Sunday.

Hot wheels: The annual cycling fundraiser for Bristol Bears Foundation took place this week and raised more than £45,000 to support the rugby charity's access and inclusion work.

Riders crossed the suspension bridge and took on Cheddar Gorge.

Trading places: The rugby team were busy, as fifty Bristol Bears players also traded rugby boots for wheelbarrows and waders as they volunteered at Bristol Zoo Project, tackling everything from clearing blanket weed from the gorilla island moat to installing new posts and ropes in the lemur walkthrough.

Blink and you'll miss it: Bristol BID (Business Improvement District) celebrated National Play Day this week by unveiling more than 30 handcrafted fairy doors hidden across Broadmead.

Not a drop in sight: Green spaces across Somerset have felt the effects of consecutive heatwaves this summer.

All across the West, grasslands have turned a yellow colour while waiting for signs of rain to come.

Natural phenomenon: A farmer in Watchet captured a waterspout which formed over the Bristol Channel.

Chris Cottrell, of Doniford Farm Park, was feeding his animals on Saturday morning when he spotted the phenomenon on the horizon.

The narrow, spinning column of air is a tornado which forms over water during showery weather conditions.

Never too old: Ninety-seven-year-old Betty Bromage strapped herself to the wing of an Aero-Super-Batics biplane in an attempt to break the Guinness World Record for the oldest female wing-walker, with her sixth wing walk, at RFC Rendcomb Airfield near Cirencester. Spoiler - she beat her own record.

Step back in time: Gloucester Cathedral has secured a £250,000 grant from the Wolfson Foundation towards the conservation of the internationally significant Great Cloister (which you might recognise from some of the Harry Potter films).

The project is helping to safeguard one of the most important examples of medieval architecture in the world.

A magical sight: Take a look at this cloud iridescence captured over Cam in Gloucestershire.

The phenomena happens when sunlight bends and scatters around microscopic, uniform droplets or ice crystals.

Lasting love: Congratulations to Peter and Betty Trotman who celebrated their 70th wedding anniversary this week, having married on 4 August 1956.

Family and friends arranged for a vintage car journey from their home in Apperley, travelling through Bishops Cleeve, past the church they were married in, then through Tewkesbury town centre before returning to Gupshill Manor, where close family and friends gathered for a celebratory lunch.

What a rescue mission: This peregrine falcon was spotted struggling in a pond. Gloucester Cathedral's team swooped in to rescue the bird and rushed it to Vale Wildlife Hospital and Rehabilitation Centre.

The falcon has now been released back into the wild after receiving the care and attention it needed.

Making ends meet: A third-generation farmer who is opening a maze to subsidise the cost of producing food says his grandfather "wouldn't be able to get his head around it".

Jeremy Stokes, who farms near Devizes in Wiltshire, said he had been forced to pull away from mainstream agriculture due to rising costs.

Better together: Locals in Chippenham gathered for a dementia-friendly picnic this week hosted by Right at Home Central Wiltshire as part of Dementia Adventure's national initiative.

Guests enjoyed bingo, storytelling, sensory experiences and a "create your own bouquet" flower bar.

Shaded sheep: The sheep of Avebury have also been feeling the effects of the recurrent heatwaves.

These ones were seeing seeking shade against the ancient stones as the hot temperatures continue across the region.

Toe-tapping concert: The High Sheriff of Wiltshire, Dr Alexander Goodwin, together with Debbie Vincent, president of Rotary Club of Swindon, have presented a cheque for £9,842.88 to Swindon domestic abuse charity Society Without Abuse.

The amount was raised in a concert which included young choristers from the JTP Trust Youth Choir and singing group Ten in A Bar.

Follow BBC West social channels in Bristol , Gloucestershire , Somerset and Wiltshire . Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630 .

headline: US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade
body:
The US military says one of its helicopters has fired missiles to disable "the steering gear" of a cargo ship attempting to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports.

In a statement, US Central Command (Centcom) says its MH-60 aircraft on Tuesday fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova vessel, as it attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman.

Centcom said it acted after "the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces". The vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran", it added.

Iran has not commented. The US has been enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, following failed attempts to end the war it and Israel started on 28 February.

Tehran retaliated by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states across the Gulf. It has also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - a key oil shipping waterway.

A fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the strait before the war and prices have fluctuated wildly since then.

Mediators have so far failed to bring the sides to an agreement on reopening the strait - and, since the latest ceasefire collapsed in June, both the US and Iran have exchanged fire intermittently.

In its statement on X, Centcom said M/V Vela attempted to sail to an Iranian port without naming it. It also did not say whether there were any casualties or injuries.

It says the US blockade "remains in full effect", adding that as of 11 August Centcom has "redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled 3 non-compliant vessels, and boarded 2".

In a separate development on Tuesday, Yemen's internationally recognised government said six people were killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they hit a vessel carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a ship since the war began.
