Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan tried to raise the alarm about 14 such sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded.

"What he told me made my blood run cold," said Hollywood actor Michael Sheen, who spoke to Gowan just months before he died and has now continued his investigation in a new BBC iPlayer documentary.

Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".

These included polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), he said, which he described as "some of the worst contaminants known to man" and were widely used during the last century, including for lipsticks and white goods.

"This stuff builds up in the environment, builds up in animals and fish, and it builds up in us," Gowan said.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.

Sheen said PCBs were now known as "the godfather of forever chemicals".

He added: "There is something out there in the forest, there is something in our bodies that can turn against us and tear us apart, but it's not like it is in the horror films. It's invisible. It's a silent killer."

These manmade chemicals are stable, resistant to extreme temperatures and pressures and have insulating properties. Because of this they were used in everything from plastics and paint to electrical equipment.

After concerns about toxicity to humans and animals were raised, a series of bans were put in place around the world from the 1970s onwards.

But the chemicals take a long time to break down and have lingered in the environment, particularly in landfill, where they can leach into waterways and then into the sea.

Gowan told Sheen in the documentary: "There was no regulation at the time, they could dump it wherever they wanted to."

In the 1980s, a fire at the lagoon at Llwyneinion near Ruabon in Wrexham took 60 firefighters more than 18 hours to bring under control.

The effects of the chemicals were reportedly felt up to 20 miles (32km) away.

Phillips and his friends went to watch, and he believes the impact of this exposure began to emerge in 2001.

"I started getting lumps on my shoulder. I caught cancer. I lost a large part of my shoulder that's literally as wide as my hand.

"While he was operating, my surgeon said 'this is strange, I've never seen this type of cancer before', and he'd had a distinguished career of 40 years."

It was not just him who was affected.

"I lost a very close friend who used to be [at the lagoon] all the time. He died of breast cancer.

"I have another friend who passed away with brain cancer. I've got another friend who is trying to get over brain cancer, I have another friend who's had all of his lymph glands taken out because they were cancerous."

Another friend has the exact type of cancer Phillips had, and his surgeon told him: "For me to catch what I had was like winning the lottery.

"For your friend who lives down the road to get exactly the same, he said it's like winning the lottery every day for six months. It's not a coincidence."

Phillips' blood tests showed higher-than-average PCB levels.

"It's chilling to think that having any PCBs in your blood is normal, when 90 years ago no-one would have had them as they didn't exist," said Sheen.

The actor also had his blood tested and it revealed 81 different types of PCBs, despite him not having lived near any dump sites.

"There is no safe level of PCBs, it's a risk all of us have to try and manage. The lower your level of PCBs, the lower your risk of getting cancer," he said.

Paul Pemberton has been a Wrexham councillor for more than 20 years and said the site had been "abused for many, many years".

Scientists found cyanide, arsenic and PCBs at the site and said it needed to be cleaned up, he said.

"We were then quoted around about £45m and that would bankrupt the council," he said.

However, Wrexham council said later investigations and risk assessments concluded that although contaminants were present, the sites did not meet the legal threshold requiring remediation.

In 2017, Gowan said the companies responsible "should be made to remediate".

Wales was not Monsanto's first choice when it came to PCB dumping.

Initially it pumped PCBs into waterways in Anniston, Alabama in the US.

In 1993, the whole town sued Monsanto for chemical contamination, resulting in one of the largest single town lawsuits in US history.

Donald Stewart, one of the attorneys involved, said it was settled for $300m.

Internal Monsanto documents showed they had been aware of the toxicity of PCBs in 1949, so how could they get away with knowingly exposing people to these chemicals?

Stewart said: "If you look at this area, it's working people. They were people who wouldn't be able to fight back."

In another memo from 1972, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor, who are helping Sheen with the investigation, found that Monsanto had decided PCBs were a worldwide problem, an environmental danger and a risk to human health, and were shutting down work at Anniston.

But then there were proposals to increase capacity to make five million more kilograms of PCBs at their plant in Newport.

"They're doing it in Newport because the legal risk in America is so much," said Ashby.

"Then the government in the UK told the industry 'we're not going to put any restrictions on importing PCBs.' So they begin importing from around the world, hundreds of tonnes of PCBs."

Gowan said: "If one wanted to be cynical about it, you could say that they were choosing places where chronic health issues might be hidden behind pre-existing health issues.

"People grew up with the knowledge that... they were in an area that had coal mining, heavy industry, the environment was contaminated, and there were health problems."

Sheen and his team took their findings to Wales' Parliament in the hope that more tests can be done.

"These people deserve more," he said.

"They deserve their concerns to be met with proper research and appropriate action. Douglas spent most of his life fighting to get the truth out there.

"The fact we all have traces of this chemical in our blood shows that we all have skin in the game. We've got to get together, we've got to fight this."

Meanwhile, members of the documentary team will appear before the Welsh Affairs Committee as it looks into alleged toxic "forever chemical" contamination in south Wales, the BBC has been told.

At a screening of the documentary, Sheen said: "These are just the places we know about... Douglas Gowan believed that there was much more."

Kirsty Luff of Friends of the Earth Cymru has called for a public inquiry into the "scale and impact of toxic sites in Wales".

She warned that climate change would make the situation worse as "more frequent and intense flooding... will bring these contaminants to the surface where they can spread over fields, they can get into water courses".

Environmental regulator Natural Resources Wales (NRW) tested Llwyneinion acid tar lagoon close to Ruabon.

Investigation work found the site did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land.

Wrexham council said because of this there was "no statutory requirement for remediation", but that it continued to carry out regular inspections and water monitoring.

It said only limited information from more recent testing had been shared with it, but it remained open to reviewing any new "robust and verifiable evidence".

NRW also said that "the legacy of historic industrial activity" in the UK and globally is an issue and as "most of this took place before modern environmental regulations were in place," the "records can be limited and the nature of waste is not always fully known."

The Welsh government said: "Addressing contaminated land is a key priority for this government.

"Our industrial heritage has left us with a difficult legacy that can affect both people and places - we want to ensure this does not pose a risk to our communities or our natural environment.

"A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation.

"While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales.

"We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."

Additional reporting by Wales environment correspondent Steffan Messenger

Buried with Michael Sheen is on BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from 17 August at 21:00 BST

headline: British driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record
body:
A British driver who was the first person to break the sound barrier in a car on land has set a new speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered vehicle.

Andy Green, a 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot, reached a speed of 406mph (654km/h) at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, the fastest a hydrogen-powered car has ever travelled.

Green's record was measured as an average of two runs in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines, with a combined 1,600 brake horsepower (bhp).

In 1997, Green drove the jet-powered ThrustSSC across Nevada's Black Rock Desert at 763mph (1,228km/h), making him the first, and still the only person, to break the sound barrier on land.

Twenty years ago, Green also set a world land speed record for a diesel vehicle in the JCB Dieselmax, attaining a speed of over 350mph (563km/h).

The new record, set in JCB's Hydromax vehicle, surpassed the previous official hydrogen combustion title set in 2004 (185.5mph) by more than double the speed.

"Setting a world land speed record with hydrogen power, 20 years after Dieselmax, is a huge privilege. This record is a huge achievement by a world class team and superb technology," Green said.

Last month, Green said his wife's encouragement was crucial in persuading him to accept the challenge after getting a call from JCB chairman Lord Anthony Bamford.

Lord Anthony said: "Twenty years ago we came to Bonneville with JCB Dieselmax and showed what British engineering could do with diesel power. Today we have done it again - this time with engines powered by hydrogen."

The company had developed the Hydromax car in an attempt to set a new record for a hydrogen-powered vehicle.

In May, the Hydromax reached 208mph (335km/h) during testing at RAF Wittering in Cambridgeshire.

headline: I share my flat with a 6ft Terminator and 30 other props
body:
Setting foot into a one-bedroom flat in an old mining village, you immediately become aware of dozens of pairs of eyes staring at you.

"My landlord used to call me Peter Pan," said 61-year-old Martin James, a former cleaner, farmer and singer who now spends much of his time buying, creating and altering his collectables.

He shares his modest-sized flat in Caerphilly county with 32 "life-sized" props, including an imposing T-800 - the Terminator played by Arnold Schwarzenegger.

He also has a 6ft, 175lb (79kg) Po, better known as Kung Fu Panda, and Pennywise, the clown from the film, It.

Overlapping action figures, posters and teddy bears also cover Martin's walls and ceilings. His collectables consist of "anything unusual", but he is mostly inspired by Hollywood.

He's far from alone and is part of a rising cohort of "kidults", who are consumers over the age of 12, who are trying to counter the "doom and gloom" of adult life, an expert said.

"They call me mad Martin and I don't know why," he laughed.

He traded his motorbike for a Terminator figure nearly 10 years ago and said his larger collectables were now increasing in value.

Martin said he was offered £10,000 for his Kung Fu Panda figure, more than the estimated value, but insists it is not about money.

"Christ, no. I'd never do it for the money. People say: 'Why collect then?' It's because I enjoy it.

"Life is too short to be boring, I don't drink, I don't smoke. If I'm going to spend any money, I'd like to show what I got out of it."

Martin's collection is a mix of rare items and props he has created or refined himself.

He says his partner has been "good as gold", helping him collect items, while his own children have grown up, allowing him to dive into his hobby.

"Kidults" represent a growing market since the pandemic, according to Elliot Riley-Walsh, creator of collection management software Valart.

People are reconnecting with childhood interests to counter the "doom and gloom" of adult life, he said.

"If you go into a Lego shop now, it's pretty much split 50-50. On your left, you've got a kids and teenagers section, and on your right, it's just a whole adult section."

Toy-sale tracking showed Kidults made up one-third of UK sales in 2025 .

Elliot cites stories of people "quitting their jobs" to invest in items like Pokémon trading cards.

"If you do it right, and if you're incredibly clever, you can make money from it," he said.

"A lot of it can sometimes boil down to luck."

Elliot, who is a collector, said social media, influencers and celebrities like Logan Paul and Henry Cavill are helping counteract a "stigma".

"Henry Cavill looks proper manly, but he's out painting Warhammer figurines.

"He's showing off his passion, I think that's one of the best things and I think it shows that human side of people."

"I think the idea of 'childlike passions', for a psychologist, we would probably label that within a broad area of play," said Dr Julie Kirkham, leader for the MSc family and child psychology programme at the University of Chester.

Kirkham places activities such as reading fiction or creative crafts in a similar category, although these might face less stigma than an activity like Lego.

"Although these may seem childlike, they may still have important functions of allowing us to be creative, to reduce stress and take a break from complex cognitive tasks and to develop social relationships and build social bonds.

"I think it's increasingly becoming recognised that adults play as well."

Kirkham also cites play as having "therapeutic value" for exploring our emotions, experiences and memories, but in a safe space.

"But it could also just be fun, sometimes it isn't any more complicated than that."

She said the pandemic created conditions for increased interest in activities like collecting.

"Humans are a very social species, so interacting via social media offered opportunities to alleviate boredom and join communities and develop friendships."

For Martin, collecting gives him a sense of meaning: "I've had a few tragedies in my life through family and whatever else, and I think, 'enjoy life while it's here'."

headline: You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check
body:
One call to your energy supplier to ensure your name is on the electricity bill may mean you are in line for a £150 discount this winter – but you need to get in before the deadline.

While the cost of heating your home might not be at the forefront of your mind during the long, hot summer prices are set to rise again this winter.

Suppliers use customers' records as of Sunday 23 August to check who is eligible for the Warm Home Discount.

The government scheme knocks £150 off bills if you are on means-tested benefits such as universal credit.

Millions of people will learn of the level of winter energy prices later this month, when Ofgem announces the quarterly price cap for the three months from October.

To help those who might struggle to pay, energy companies distribute the £150 Warm Home Discount to about six million households in the winter. Households in receipt of housing benefit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and universal credit qualify.

Households who are eligible should get the discount automatically, provided their supplier has over 1,000 customers.

However, that only happens if your name is on the bill and you are receiving one of these benefits. It can also help suppliers offer better support, such as repayment plans, to those who have energy debt.

Someone might not be named on their electricity bill if they have recently moved house.

Eligible customers on pre-payment meters who use a key or card to top up will also need to ensure that their household's account is registered in their name.

"If you know someone who might benefit, please start spreading the word and encourage them to check they are named on their energy bill," said Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

The government added that 345,000 Scottish low-income households who are also classed as vulnerable would now automatically receive the rebate in the winter. This would usually be having a child under five in the household, having a disability or getting a pensioner premium with the benefit.

Other low income households in Scotland will still have to apply through their energy supplier.

headline: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
body:
The first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.

Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.

The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".

The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".

The Game of Thrones origin story is epic in both ambition and execution – it has taken seven years to reach the stage, clocks in at three hours 45 minutes, and features a 36-strong cast.

The characters include younger versions of familiar figures like Ned Stark, Jaime Lannister and Robert Baratheon; and others whose fates were key to the events in the main saga, such as Lyanna Stark, Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and the "mad king" himself, Aerys II Targaryen.

After opening in Shakespeare's home town, the RSC will hope it can go on to replicate the success of other spin-off plays like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Stranger Things: The First Shadow, which have both had lengthy runs in the West End and on Broadway.

The Shakespeare connection stems from the fact Martin's novels were heavily inspired by Shakespeare's history plays, especially those about the battles between the houses of Lancaster and York during the Wars of the Roses in the 15th Century.

Game of Thrones' US creator was heavily involved in the play, stationing a representative in rehearsals at all times, and he attended the opening night in Stratford on Saturday.

In the Guardian's review, Mark Lawson wrote : "Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist's royal dramas plain.

"The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences."

Audiences will respond differently to the play depending on whether they are already loyal Game of Thrones fans, and Lawson's four-star rating attempted to bridge that gap.

"This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven't seen the TV series," he said.

Metro's critic Dave Freak agreed , also bestowing four stars.

"As a stand-alone piece of theatre, The Mad King scrapes through," he wrote. "But as an extension of the Game of Thrones world, it scores well, shifting the narrative to the stage with suitably theatrical thrust."

The Telegraph's Dominic Cavendish wrote : "At almost four hours, it's a long evening, sometimes too dense with detail, and it lacks the grit and gore (not to mention the nudity) of the TV series.

"Still, it capably serves newbies and devotees, and speaks in a timely fashion to our age of unruly leaders."

He added: "It's not up there, yet, with the Harry Potter or Stranger Things prequels but, on balance, the Game of Thrones franchise has yet another worthwhile and lucrative spin-off on its hands."

The Times' critic Clive Davis had greater reservations, writing that while the play "gives hardcore GoT fans a chance to go hunting for 'Easter eggs', it seldom comes close to matching the grim aura of the TV series".

He wrote: "Duncan Macmillan's script is sorely lacking in poetry. Events plod forward, one after the other, and although Michael Shaeffer is a thoroughly compelling presence as the cruel and chronically unstable monarch Aerys, other performances seem nuance-free. Too many lines are simply shouted. You expect better of the RSC."

Davis concluded: "It goes without saying that there are more than enough GoT devotees to keep the box office ticking over for the rest of eternity, but only the most dedicated of them will have the energy for this marathon."

Others were more enthusiastic, and Whatsonstage's Sarah Crompton's five-star review said the play is "a triumph; a soaring, surging spectacle and a latter-day history play, both serious and popular".

She added: "It is a remarkable achievement, wonderfully directed by [Dominic] Cooke and superbly acted by every member of the 35-strong ensemble. The result is a brilliant exhibition of how theatre can create magic."

The Independent's Alice Saville , awarding four stars, said the "stellar stage show has all the thrillingly staged battles, gory deaths and, yes, dragons that the most bloodthirsty fan could hope for".

"But there's also a surprising amount of heart – of the warm, still-beating kind – as it lingers on the faces of its fallen," she said.

The play begins more than a decade before the events in the first book and TV series, opening with the tourney at Harrenhal, a great jousting tournament where the houses of the Seven Kingdoms gathered and where key events in the Game of Thrones legend took place.

Macmillan said he wanted to create something "on the scale of a Shakespearean tragedy and a Shakespearean history".

The playwright told BBC News: "The challenge was writing something for a fan base who take this world and their characters very, very seriously and know so much about it, and also the complete newbies, and writing something that is going to work for both of those people.

"Making something that is going to knock the socks off of everybody has been a real challenge. It's taken a long time, but I think we've got there."

Cooke said there were "lots of similarities" with Shakespeare, especially the themes of "dynastic struggle, what it means to have power, intergenerational conflict and powerful families".

Martin has been "very supportive" in the process of creating the play, the director added.

"He's been collaborative in terms of the development of the script. We've worked very closely with him. And George, I think, picked up quite quickly that we were very serious about honouring what he'd done."

Tamara Harvey, the RSC's co-artistic director, said: "George himself talks about how Shakespeare and the Wars of the Roses inspired him to write these stories.

"So the connections feel very deep, and of course themes are shared: power, love, succession, battles for who gets to rule who – it's all there in the Shakespeare history, just as it is in Game of Thrones."

Asked about future plans for the play, Harvey replied: "We're hoping as many people as possible get to see it, and that starts here in Stratford. And from then, who knows?"

headline: At least 44 die as ferry sinks in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba
body:
At least 44 people have died after a ferry sank on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe on Tuesday, police have said.

The ferry had a capacity to carry 90 passengers and five crew members but a lake official had reported that 120 people, including 12 children, were on it.

The vessel was hit by a strong wave and overturned, police added. Footage shared online appears to show the overturned hull floating in the water.

President Emmerson Mnangagwa has declared a state of disaster, as search and rescue operations intensify. So far, 77 people have been rescued.

Lake Kariba, which straddles the border with Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs, supporting transport and fishing and providing vital hydroelectric power to both countries.

An eyewitness, Maxton Kanhema, told AFP news agency that the boat had travelled in bad weather and may have been hit by a wave, causing its engines to switch off.

"People were in distress... there were bodies in the water and it was a sad situation to witness. Those that could be rescued were rescued," he was quoted as saying.

Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video on X of what she said was the boat at the start of the journey, adding that residents had been travelling across the lake to Kariba town, about five hours away.

"We have very hard questions that require honest answers. The officials must release the correct number of people who were onboard," she wrote.

The Zimbabwe Civil Protection Unit (CPU) said that registered ticket sales showed 114 adult passengers were on the vessel. An unknown number of children below ticketing age could also have been onboard, it added.

In its latest update on X , police said that 44 bodies had now been retrieved from the lake - up from the initial 15.

Local government minister Daniel Garwe said the president had declared a state of disaster to ensure "all necessary resources are mobilised" for search and rescue operations.

This included an army boat squadron, a police sub-aqua unit and a privately owned helicopter, he said.

"The government extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives in this tragic incident," Garwe added in a statement.

headline: Brother of man trapped under rubble in Colombian quake clings on to hope
body:
Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure.

"You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.

His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.

This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.

The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.

Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.

Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.

On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."

The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.

These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.

Torres del Limonar is one of more than 50 collapsed buildings in Cali.

It is located in its south, in the Capri neighbourhood. The four-storey building held dozens of apartments. The exact number of tenants who were inside when it collapsed is unknown.

Around it, apart from some cracks, the rest of the buildings seem to have escaped the fate of the Torres.

Rescuers, military personnel, volunteers, paramedics, firefighters, humanitarian workers, and journalists have come here.

There are more than 100 people waiting for news. According to Mayor Éder, as of Monday night, it was estimated that 25 people were trapped under the rubble.

Éder declared a nighttime curfew to speed up rescue operations.

The night passed. Excavations continue. A rescuer at the site said about 10 people had been saved since the collapse.

Reports in local media, such as one from Blu Pacífico radio, spoke of six survivors up until a few minutes before my arrival, including an infant only a few months old.

In the midst of tragedy, figures are often closer to estimates than definitive data.

"What I can tell you is that right now there are at least two people detected alive. Tunnels are being made to get them out. One of them has to have his leg freed," rescuer James Velasco tells me.

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday, 10 August, is the worst in this century, according to the National Geological Service.

In addition to Cali, it left destruction and death in other regions such as Chocó, in the north-west.

Around the remains of Torres del Limonar, unlike Gallego, many residents choose not to speak. They are visibly affected.

Some sleep exhausted on the ground or on a sofa placed in the street. Others gather together under the shade for support.

The hours are long, increasingly so, and the anguish grows.

Velasco offers hope.

"In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped."

"Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds.

"I wanted to help from the very beginning."

Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens.

"We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.

Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock.

"I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains.

Together with several friends, Mahecha helps remove rubble, bring water to rescuers, and clear the street to facilitate evacuation efforts.

In the background, hammers and saws can be heard creating escape routes through the destruction.

They stop only when those present raise their arms.

That means everyone must remain silent. Gallego waits. This time, too, there was no news of his brother.
